teile.einleitung: Cones are the woody seed structures of conifers such as firs, spruces, pines or larches. The seeds ripen between their scales. What is fascinating is that cones open and close all by themselves, depending on whether the weather is dry or damp.
wichtigste: Cones grow on conifers and carry the seeds under their scales.
In dry weather a cone opens its scales so that the winged seeds can fly away.
To open and close, the cone needs nothing but a change in humidity.
The scales bend because two layers of tissue swell to different degrees.
The cones of the silver fir stand upright on the branches.
Most of the cones on the floor of Swiss forests come from the spruce.
Squirrels like to get the seeds out of the cones.

abschnitte.text: A cone is a seed structure, that is, the part of a **conifer** in which the seeds develop. It consists of an axis around which many woody **scales** are arranged in a spiral. Under each scale there are usually two seeds, each with a small wing. Depending on the type of tree, it takes from a few months to two years for a cone to ripen.

When the air is dry, the scales spread apart and the seeds can fall out. In rain or fog they close again, because wet seeds would not fly far. This works because each scale consists of **two layers** that swell to different degrees when damp. The cone needs no energy and no living cells for this; even a cone that has fallen off still moves.

In everyday German almost all cones are called “Tannenzapfen” (fir cones), but that is usually wrong. The **silver fir** carries its cones upright at the top of the crown. When they are ripe, the scales fall off one by one, and only the spindle stays on the branch. The **spruce**, on the other hand, has hanging cones that fall to the ground whole. That is why almost all the cones you find in a Swiss forest are spruce cones.

The seeds in the cones are nutritious and popular with many animals. The **squirrel** gnaws off the scales and leaves behind a frayed spindle. Mice, on the other hand, gnaw the cones neatly and smoothly. The **common crossbill** is a bird with a crossed beak, which it uses to skilfully get seeds out of the cones. Woodpeckers also wedge cones into cracks in trees to peck them open.

Researchers have taken the movement of cones as a model; this is called **biomimetics**. This led to the idea of fabrics that open small air holes when you sweat and close again as they dry. Building fronts that open by themselves depending on the weather are also being developed on this principle. Some people even use cones as simple weather indicators.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tree with needles instead of broad leaves, for example spruce, fir or pine.
A woody plate on the cone under which the seeds lie.
The central axis of a cone on which the scales sit.
Technology that copies ideas from nature.

gewusst: A cone can still open and close even after years if you alternately make it wet and let it dry.
You almost never find whole silver fir cones on the ground, because they already fall apart on the tree.
The cones of some pine species in North America only open after a forest fire, because of the heat.

teile.einleitung: T cells are white blood cells and are among the most important fighters in our immune system. They recognise cells that have been infected by viruses or have turned into cancer cells, and they help to get rid of them. They are named after the thymus, the organ in which they mature.
wichtigste: T cells are a group of white blood cells, the lymphocytes.
They mature in the thymus, which shrinks over the course of life.
Helper T cells carry the marker CD4 on their surface.
Cytotoxic CD8 T cells kill infected or abnormal body cells.
A T-cell receptor recognises a small piece of protein that is presented on an MHC molecule.
HIV mainly attacks CD4 helper T cells.
In 2025 the Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded for discoveries about regulatory T cells.

abschnitte.text: T cells are **lymphocytes**, a type of white blood cell. They come from stem cells in the bone marrow and then travel to the **thymus**, an organ behind the breastbone. After that they patrol through the blood and lymph and stay in lymph nodes and the spleen. They belong to the acquired immune defence, which can remember particular pathogens.

In the thymus, the young T cells learn to tell foreign from self. In **negative selection**, T cells that react strongly to the body's own substances are removed. This prevents them from attacking the body itself. Only a small part of the cells passes this strict test. In children the thymus is large; later it shrinks and is partly replaced by fat.

Every T cell carries a **T-cell receptor**, which, like a lock, only fits one particular key. Body cells show small pieces of protein on their surface on so-called **MHC molecules**, rather like identity cards. If such a piece comes from a virus, the matching T cell recognises the danger. Then it multiplies strongly and forms a whole army of identical cells.

**Helper T cells** with the marker CD4 pass on commands to other defence cells, for example to the B cells, which make antibodies. **Cytotoxic T cells** with CD8 kill infected cells directly. Regulatory T cells put the brakes on the immune system so that it does not overreact. Memory T cells stay in the body for years and react much faster the next time they meet the same pathogen. This is also what makes many vaccinations work.

**HIV** mainly destroys helper T cells and so weakens the whole immune system. In **CAR T-cell therapy**, T cells from cancer patients are given a new receptor against tumour cells in the laboratory and returned to the body. In 2025 Mary Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell and Shimon Sakaguchi received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for their research on regulatory T cells. These cells help to prevent the immune system from attacking the body itself.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of white blood cells that includes T cells and B cells.
An organ behind the breastbone in which T cells mature.
A feature by which the immune system recognises something foreign.
A protein on the cell surface that shows small pieces of protein like an identity card.
A disease in which the immune system attacks the body itself.

gewusst: There are so many different T-cell receptors in the body that almost any imaginable pathogen can be recognised by some T cell.
The letter T in the name stands for thymus.
For a long time the thymus was thought to be a useless organ, until its task was discovered in the 1960s.

teile.einleitung: A stethoscope is a device that doctors use to listen to sounds inside the body, for example your heartbeat. It is one of the best-known tools in medicine. With it you can also hear how the air flows in the lungs.
wichtigste: With a stethoscope you listen to the heart, lungs and intestines.
Listening in this way is called auscultation.
It was invented in 1816 by the French doctor René Laënnec.
A stethoscope consists of a chest piece, tubes and earpieces.
It does not amplify sounds electrically but carries the sound along.
A stethoscope is often also used when measuring blood pressure.

abschnitte.text: The stethoscope is a listening device for examining the body. The name comes from Greek: stethos means chest and skopein means to look at. Doctors often wear it around their neck. Listening with a stethoscope is called **auscultation** in technical language.

At the front is the **chest piece**, usually with a thin membrane and a small funnel. When it is placed on the skin, the membrane vibrates with the sounds inside the body. The sound travels through the **tubes** to the ear tubes with soft earpieces. Because hardly any sounds from outside get in, you hear the quiet sounds much more clearly.

At the heart you hear the **heart sounds**, which are made when the heart valves close. It sounds a bit like “ba-boom”. In the lungs you hear the rushing of the air you breathe, and with pneumonia often crackling or rattling too. On the tummy, a gurgling sound shows that the intestines are working.

In 1816 the French doctor **René Laënnec** in Paris wanted to examine a young patient. At that time doctors put their ear directly on the chest, which made him feel uncomfortable. He rolled a sheet of paper into a tube and suddenly heard the heart much more loudly. From this he developed a wooden listening tube, and later tubes and two earpieces were added.

When **measuring blood pressure**, a cuff is put around the upper arm and pumped up. With the stethoscope in the crook of the elbow you hear when the blood starts to flow again and when the knocking disappears. This gives the two values of blood pressure. Today there are also automatic devices for this that do not need a stethoscope.

As well as classic stethoscopes, there are **electronic stethoscopes**, which can amplify and record sounds. This means heart sounds can be saved or sent to other experts. Despite ultrasound and other modern devices, the stethoscope remains important. It is cheap, ready to use quickly and needs no electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: Listening to sounds inside the body with a stethoscope.
A valve in the heart that makes sure the blood flows in only one direction.
A thin, vibrating disc that picks up sound.
The pressure with which the blood pushes against the walls of the blood vessels.

gewusst: The first stethoscope was simply a rolled-up sheet of paper.
Many doctors warm the chest piece in their hand before listening, because otherwise it feels cold on the skin.
Vets also use stethoscopes, even on elephants.

teile.einleitung: A bull is an adult male of the cattle family. Bulls are big and strong and can weigh more than a tonne. In Switzerland, people often call a bull “Muni” in Swiss German.
wichtigste: An adult male of the cattle family is called a bull.
Cattle can hardly see the colour red.
In a bullfight, the bull is provoked by the movement of the cloth, not by its colour.
The red cloth in a bullfight is called a muleta, and the bullfighter is a matador.
Bullfights are especially well known in Spain.
The eyes of cattle are on the sides of their head.
The German saying “Das ist für ihn ein rotes Tuch” (that is a red cloth to him) means: that makes him very angry.

abschnitte.text: A bull is a fully grown **male of the cattle family**. It is usually bigger and much more muscular than a cow, with a powerful neck and a broad forehead. A large bull can weigh more than a tonne. In many breeds bulls have horns, but there are also hornless breeds.

The eyes of cattle are **on the sides of the head**. This means they can see almost all the way round themselves without turning their head. Only directly behind them can they see nothing. Cattle see fewer colours than we do; they can hardly make out **red**, but they react very sensitively to movement.

Bullfights are especially well known in **Spain**, but they also take place in Portugal, southern France and Latin America. The **matador** waves a red cloth called the **muleta**. What provokes the bull is the movement of the cloth, not its colour. Bullfights are very controversial because the bull is injured and often killed, and animal fights of this kind are banned in Switzerland.

In Swiss German the bull is called **Muni**. At the Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival, the winner traditionally receives a live bull as a prize, the **Siegermuni** (winner's bull). Usually, though, the wrestling king lets the bull go on living on a farm. In Valais there are also the well-known fights of the Hérens cows, in which the cows measure their strength without any people taking part.

The German saying “Das ist für ihn ein **rotes Tuch**” (that is a red cloth to him) means that something makes him very angry. “To take the bull by the horns” means to tackle a difficult problem bravely. On the stock exchange, the bull stands for rising prices. In the sky there is also the constellation of Taurus, the Bull, with the bright red star Aldebaran.

Bulls can be very strong and sometimes unpredictable. That is why on farms they often wear a **nose ring**, by which they can be led safely. When hiking, you should cross pastures with cattle calmly and keep your distance. This is especially important when dogs are with you or when there are calves in the pasture.

begriffe.erklaerung: Large hoofed animals with horns that are kept as farm animals.
The Swiss German word for a bull.
The bullfighter who waves the red cloth in a bullfight.
The red cloth used in a bullfight.

gewusst: A bull would also charge at a blue or green cloth if it were moved.
The winner's bull at the Federal Wrestling Festival is always given its own name.
The famous bronze statue “Charging Bull” on Wall Street in New York shows a bull ready to attack.

teile.einleitung: The Swatch is a colourful Swiss plastic wristwatch that came onto the market in 1983. It was cheap and fashionable and helped the Swiss watch industry out of a severe crisis. Today the brand belongs to the Swatch Group in Biel, one of the largest watch companies in the world.
wichtigste: The first Swatch came onto the market in 1983 and was presented in Zurich.
The case of a classic Swatch is made of plastic.
The name combines “Second” and “Watch”.
Nicolas G. Hayek is regarded as the “father of the Swatch”.
Swatch watches are especially known for their bright colours and patterns.
New collections appear about every six months.
The Swatch helped to save the Swiss watch industry.

abschnitte.text: A **Swatch** is a light quartz watch with a plastic case. Compared with classic watches it consists of far fewer parts, only 51. The case is welded shut, so you cannot simply open it. This meant it could be produced in large numbers and at a low price.

In the 1970s, cheap **quartz watches** from Japan and other countries came onto the market. Many Swiss watch companies got into difficulty, and tens of thousands of people lost their jobs. This is known as the **quartz crisis**. The Swiss watch industry needed a new idea to become successful again.

Engineers at the company ETA in Grenchen, including Elmar Mock and Jacques Müller, developed the new plastic watch at the beginning of the 1980s. On 1 March 1983 the Swatch was presented in Zurich. At the same time, the businessman **Nicolas G. Hayek** brought the struggling watch companies together into a new group and made the Swatch famous around the world. That is why he is regarded as the “father of the Swatch”.

Swatch watches come in countless colours, patterns and designs, often created by artists. New **collections** appear about every six months. Many people own not just one Swatch but collect several. Rare models are traded among collectors for high prices.

In 1998 Hayek's merger of companies became the **Swatch Group**, based in Biel in the canton of Bern. It includes many well-known brands such as Omega, Longines, Tissot and Rado. Since the death of Nicolas G. Hayek in 2010, his children have continued to run the company. Today the Swatch is regarded as a symbol of Swiss inventiveness and design.

begriffe.erklaerung: A watch in which a tiny vibrating quartz crystal sets the beat.
A severe crisis of the Swiss watch industry in the 1970s and 1980s.
A series of new models that come out together.
The cover of a watch that protects the movement.

gewusst: In 1998 Swatch invented “Internet Time”, which divided the day into 1000 “beats” instead of hours.
A classic Swatch consists of only 51 parts.
In 2022 Swatch, together with Omega, brought out the MoonSwatch, and long queues formed outside its shops.

teile.einleitung: Diving means going below the surface of the water to explore the underwater world, do research or work. With a compressed air cylinder, divers can stay underwater for a long time. Important safety rules apply, because humans are not fish.
wichtigste: In scuba diving you usually breathe compressed air from a cylinder.
Fins on your feet help you move forward.
The mask makes sure that you can see clearly underwater.
A wetsuit made of neoprene keeps you warm.
You should never dive alone.
Divers have to come up slowly, otherwise they can become ill.
Underwater, divers communicate with hand signals.

abschnitte.text: In **freediving**, you simply hold your breath, as when snorkelling or diving in the swimming pool. In **scuba diving**, you carry a cylinder of compressed air on your back. Through a hose and a mouthpiece, the regulator, you get the air to breathe. Depending on the depth, you can stay underwater for half an hour or longer.

A **mask** over your eyes and nose makes sure you can see clearly, because without air in front of your eyes everything looks blurred underwater. **Fins** on your feet make swimming much easier. A suit made of **neoprene** keeps you warm, because water draws heat away from the body quickly. There is also a jacket for floating in the water, weights and a depth gauge or dive computer.

The deeper you dive, the harder the water presses; every 10 metres adds about as much **pressure** as the whole air above us. That is why you have to equalise the pressure in your ears. Under pressure, more nitrogen from the air you breathe dissolves in the blood. If you come up too fast, gas bubbles form in the body, like in an opened bottle of sparkling water; this is called **decompression sickness**.

The most important rule is: never dive alone, but always with a **dive partner**, your buddy. You cannot speak underwater, so you communicate with **hand signals**. For example, thumb and index finger forming a ring means “everything is OK”. Before you dive with a cylinder, you have to take a diving course with a test.

In 1943 the Frenchman **Jacques-Yves Cousteau**, together with Émile Gagnan, developed a practical breathing device for divers. He became world-famous with his films about the underwater world. In 1960 the Swiss **Jacques Piccard** dived into the Mariana Trench in the submersible Trieste, which his father Auguste Piccard had developed. There, almost 11,000 metres down, is the deepest point of the world's oceans.

There is a lot of diving in Switzerland too, for example in Lake Zurich, Lake Thun or Lake Maggiore. Underwater you find fish such as pike and perch, but also old shipwrecks. Because the lakes are cold, many divers wear thick **drysuits**. In mountain lakes you also have to take the altitude into account, because the air pressure is lower there.

begriffe.erklaerung: Diving with a cylinder of breathing air on your back.
Diving while holding your breath, without any breathing apparatus.
The device that delivers the air from the cylinder in a way that you can breathe it in.
A soft, insulating rubber material for diving suits.
An illness caused by gas bubbles in the body after coming up too fast.

gewusst: Underwater, colours disappear little by little; just a few metres down, red already looks almost grey.
On his dive into the Mariana Trench, Jacques Piccard went deeper than anyone before him.
Sound travels about four times faster underwater than in air, which is why you can hardly tell where a noise is coming from.

teile.einleitung: The penny bun, also called the cep or porcini, is one of the best-known and most popular edible mushrooms in Europe. It has a brown cap, a thick stem and fine tubes under the cap instead of gills. Mushroom pickers in Switzerland are delighted every late summer and autumn when they find a penny bun.
wichtigste: The penny bun has fine tubes under its cap instead of gills.
Its cap is brown.
The stem of a young penny bun is thick and bulging.
In German it is called “Steinpilz” (stone mushroom) because its flesh is very firm.
The penny bun grows in woods and is a very popular edible mushroom.
In Italian it is called porcino.
So that it can be kept for a long time, it is often dried.

abschnitte.text: The cap of the penny bun is **brown**, often like a freshly baked bread roll, and can grow more than 20 centimetres wide. Under the cap there are fine **tubes**, which are white in young mushrooms and later yellowish to olive green. The **stem** of young mushrooms is thick and bulging and has a fine, pale net pattern. Its flesh is white and very firm, which is where the German name “Steinpilz” (stone mushroom) comes from.

The penny bun grows in **woods**, especially under spruces, beeches, oaks and pines. It lives in a partnership with the roots of these trees, which is called **mycorrhiza**. The mushroom supplies the tree with water and mineral salts, and in return the tree gives it sugar. That is why you never find penny buns in an open meadow without trees.

In Switzerland you find penny buns mainly from summer into autumn, especially after warm rain. They grow in the Central Plateau as well as in mountain forests up to the tree line. Many cantons have **mushroom protection rules**, for example a maximum amount per person per day or days when picking is not allowed. The rules differ from canton to canton.

The penny bun can be confused with the **bitter bolete**, which tastes very bitter. Its tubes turn pink with age, and its stem has a dark net. Just one bitter bolete can make a whole mushroom dish inedible. That is why you should always have mushrooms you have picked checked at an official **mushroom inspection**, which exists in many Swiss municipalities.

Because of its nutty flavour, the penny bun is a very popular **edible mushroom**. You can fry it, use it in risotto or pasta, or cook it as a soup. Penny buns are often dried, because dried they keep for a long time and taste especially strong. In Italy it is called **porcino**, and risotto ai porcini is also a well-known dish in Ticino.

abschnitte.titel: A mushroom that cannot be farmed
abschnitte.text: Button mushrooms can be grown on compost in large sheds, but so far this has not really worked with the penny bun. The reason is its close partnership with living trees. So almost all penny buns sold in shops come from mushrooms picked in the wild. Dried penny buns often come from Eastern Europe or China.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mushroom that has fine tubes under its cap instead of gills.
A partnership between fungi and plant roots from which both benefit.
A mushroom that you can eat.
A place where experts check picked mushrooms for poisonous ones.

gewusst: The scientific name Boletus edulis means something like “edible bolete”.
A large penny bun can weigh more than one kilogram.
Porcino means “little pig” in Italian.

teile.einleitung: Survivorship bias is a mistake in thinking: you look only at the cases that have made it through a selection and forget all the others. As a result, many things seem better, more solid or more successful than they really are. If you know about this mistake, you are less likely to fall for wrong conclusions.
wichtigste: With survivorship bias, you look only at cases that have made it through a selection.
A survey of only the current members of a gym is biased, because unhappy members have already left.
Investment funds look more successful in hindsight, because bad funds are closed and drop out of the statistics.
Old houses seem more solid, because the badly built ones disappeared long ago.
Successful university dropouts do not prove that dropping out leads to success, because the many unsuccessful dropouts are missing.
Old music often seems better, because only the best songs are remembered.
You avoid the mistake by also including failed or eliminated cases.

abschnitte.text: **Survivorship bias** is a distortion that arises when you only look at the “survivors” of a selection. The cases that dropped out, failed or disappeared are missing from the picture. Because they are invisible, they are easily forgotten. This leads to wrong conclusions about causes and chances of success.

A famous example comes from the Second World War. Bombers that had returned were examined, and people wanted to add more armour to the places with lots of bullet holes. The statistician **Abraham Wald** pointed out that they were only seeing the aircraft that had come back despite being hit. So it was precisely the places without holes that should be armoured, because aircraft hit there had crashed.

Someone says: “Houses used to be built much more solidly; after all, the old ones are still standing today.” But you no longer see the badly built houses, because they were demolished or collapsed long ago. In a similar way, the music of past decades often seems better, because only the best songs have stayed in our **memory**. A survey of the current members of a gym is also biased, because unhappy members have already left.

Self-help books like to show successful entrepreneurs who dropped out of university. But the conclusion “dropping out leads to success” is questionable, because the many unsuccessful dropouts are missing from these books. It is similar with **investment funds**: bad funds are closed and drop out of the statistics. The remaining ones look more successful in hindsight than the average of all funds was.

abschnitte.titel: The cats from the tower block
abschnitte.text: Vets in New York found that cats seemed to survive falls from very high floors better than from medium ones. One possible explanation takes survivorship bias into account. Cats that died in a fall hardly ever came to the **vet's surgery** and were therefore missing from the statistics. The example shows that you always have to ask which cases do not appear in the data at all.

The best way to avoid the mistake is to also include **failed** or eliminated cases. That is why researchers ask: who dropped out of the group, and why? In studies, for example, participants who left early are counted too. In everyday life, a simple question helps: what am I actually not seeing here?

begriffe.erklaerung: A distortion or prejudice; in German it is called “Verzerrung”.
A typical error when reasoning that leads to wrong conclusions.
A selection of cases that is studied.
A pot into which many people pay money, which is invested in shares or other assets.

gewusst: Abraham Wald came from Klausenburg, today's Cluj in Romania, and fled to the USA before the Second World War.
With lottery winners, too, you almost only hear about those who won, never about the millions who lost.
The picture of an aircraft with red dots for bullet holes has become a well-known symbol of this mistake in thinking on the internet.

teile.einleitung: A sample is a small selection from a larger group that is examined more closely. From the result you then draw conclusions about the whole group, just as when cooking you taste a spoonful of soup to find out how the whole pot tastes.
wichtigste: A sample is a selection from a larger group.
The whole group in question is called the population.
Samples save time and money.
A representative sample reflects the population well.
In a random sample, every element has the same chance of being chosen.
Larger samples usually give more reliable results.
If only one particular group is asked, the sample is biased.

abschnitte.text: In statistics you often want to know something about a large group, the **population**. This could be all the children at a school, all the voters in Switzerland or all the apples in a harvest. Instead of examining all of them, you choose a part, the **sample**. This is quicker, costs less and is sometimes the only possibility, for example when products have to be destroyed during testing.

A good sample is **representative**, which means that it reflects the population well. If you want to know which sport young people in Switzerland like best, you must not only ask members of a football club. Otherwise the sample is **biased**, and the result is not true for everyone. So you have to ask young people from different regions, age groups and interests.

A safe way is the **random sample**. In it, every element of the population has the same chance of being chosen, as in a draw from a lottery drum. In this way nobody is favoured and nobody is forgotten. The larger the sample, the more reliable the result usually is, because chance effects even out better.

If 50 out of 200 people answer yes in a survey, that is 25 per cent. If, in a sample of 100 pupils, 30 come by bike, that is 30 per cent. For a whole school with 600 children you would then estimate that about 180 come by bike. Such an estimate is called a **projection**, and it is never completely accurate.

When there are votes in Switzerland, research institutes publish **projections** as early as Sunday afternoon, based on the municipalities that have already been counted. Surveys before elections usually ask a few thousand people instead of all voters. Food inspectors test samples of goods in the laboratory. In medicine, too, new medicines are first tested on a sample of volunteers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The whole group that you want to find something out about.
Standing well for the whole.
A selection in which every element has the same chance of being drawn.
An error that occurs when a sample does not reflect the population correctly.

gewusst: The German word for sample, “Stichprobe”, comes from metal smelting, where molten metal from a tapped furnace was tested.
Even a well-chosen sample of about a thousand people can allow fairly accurate statements about a whole country.

teile.einleitung: Camouflage means that an animal looks like its surroundings so that it is not discovered. Some animals are adapted in colour, others look like twigs or leaves. Camouflage helps animals hide from enemies, but also to creep up on prey.
wichtigste: Camouflage helps animals not to be discovered so easily.
The mountain hare and the rock ptarmigan get a white coat in winter.
The stoat turns white in winter, and only the tip of its tail stays black.
Young roe deer have white spots in their fur for camouflage.
The chameleon can change the colour of its skin.
The stick insect looks like a thin twig.
The leaf insect looks like a green leaf.

abschnitte.text: With **camouflage**, an animal matches its surroundings in colour, pattern or shape. An enemy or a prey animal then easily overlooks it. For prey animals this means protection from predators. Hunters such as tigers or owls, on the other hand, use camouflage to creep up unnoticed.

abschnitte.titel: White winter coats in the Alps
abschnitte.text: In the Swiss Alps, some animals change their coat in autumn. The **mountain hare** gets a white winter coat, and the **rock ptarmigan** wears white feathers in winter. The **stoat**, a small member of the weasel family, also turns white, and only the tip of its tail stays black. In spring all three become brown or grey-spotted again, to match rocks and earth.

Young roe deer, the fawns, have white spots in their brown fur. When they lie in the grass, the pattern looks like spots of sunlight falling through leaves. Zebra stripes or leopard spots break up the outline of the body; this is called **disruptive colouration**. Many fish are dark on top and pale underneath, so they are hard to see from above and from below.

Some animals imitate objects from their surroundings; this is called **mimesis**. The **stick insect** looks like a thin twig and even moves with a rocking motion like a twig in the wind. The **leaf insect** is green and flat and has veins like a real leaf. Some caterpillars look like bird droppings, so that nobody wants to eat them.

The **chameleon** can change the colour of its skin; for this it has special cells with tiny crystals in its skin. But it does not change colour only for camouflage, but also depending on its mood and the temperature. The real masters are cuttlefish and octopuses, which change colour and pattern in fractions of a second. Flatfish such as the plaice even adapt to the pattern of the seabed.

Humans use camouflage too, for example soldiers with **camouflage suits** in mottled patterns. Hunters and wildlife photographers hide behind camouflage nets to watch wild animals. The models for this come from nature. Researchers are even developing fabrics that can change their colour like a chameleon.

begriffe.erklaerung: The way an animal matches its surroundings so that it is not discovered.
An animal imitates an object, for example a twig or a leaf.
Patterns such as stripes or spots visually break up the outline of the body.
The fur or feathers that an animal wears in winter.

gewusst: The polar bear actually has black skin; its fur only looks white.
Because of climate change there is often less snow in the Alps, and then white mountain hares stand out especially on brown ground.
Some octopuses can change not only their colour but also the surface of their skin, so that it looks rough like a stone.

teile.einleitung: Taphonomy is the science of what happens to a living thing after its death, until perhaps it becomes a fossil. It explains why some animals and plants are preserved for millions of years while others vanish without a trace. In this way it helps researchers to interpret fossils correctly.
wichtigste: Taphonomy studies the processes from the death of a living thing to its fossilisation.
The term was introduced by the Soviet researcher Ivan Yefremov in 1940.
Biostratinomy studies the time between death and burial in sediment.
Living things with hard shells are heavily overrepresented in the fossil record.
Soft parts are most likely to be preserved if they are buried quickly without oxygen.
Petrified wood forms through permineralisation, for example with silica.
A steinkern, or internal mould, is the hardened filling of a shell.

abschnitte.text: The word **taphonomy** comes from Greek and means something like “the study of burial”. It was introduced in 1940 by the Soviet palaeontologist **Ivan Yefremov**, who also wrote science fiction novels. Taphonomy studies all the processes from the death of a living thing to its **fossilisation**. It is part of palaeontology, the science of the living things of prehistoric times.

The branch called **biostratinomy** studies the time between death and burial in sediment. During this time, scavengers feed on the body, bacteria break it down, and water can wash parts away. For something to be preserved, the body must be covered quickly by **sediment** such as mud, sand or volcanic ash. This works best in calm water with little oxygen.

**Hard parts** such as shells, bones and teeth break down much more slowly than skin, muscles or organs. That is why mussels, snails and ammonites are heavily overrepresented in the fossil record. Jellyfish or worms, on the other hand, only rarely become fossils. Soft parts are preserved mainly when they are buried quickly in a **low-oxygen** environment.

In **permineralisation**, dissolved minerals such as silica get into cavities and turn them to stone; this is how petrified wood forms. If the inside of a shell fills with sediment that hardens, a **steinkern** (internal mould) is formed. In **carbonisation**, plant remains sealed off from the air turn into a thin film of carbon. Small insects can also be completely enclosed in amber.

Places with especially well-preserved fossils are called **fossil Lagerstätten**. In Switzerland, these include **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino, where marine reptiles and fish from the Triassic period have been found. It has been a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site since 2003. In Germany the Messel Pit is well known, where even feathers and stomach contents of prehistoric animals have been preserved.

begriffe.erklaerung: A petrified remain or a trace of a living thing from earlier ages of the Earth.
Deposited material such as mud, sand or limestone that turns into rock over time.
Minerals fill the cavities of a remain and turn it into stone.
A fossil made of hardened sediment that has filled the inside of a shell.
The science of the living things of past ages of the Earth.

gewusst: Only a tiny fraction of all the living things that have ever lived have been preserved as fossils.
Ivan Yefremov was not only a researcher but also a well-known science fiction author.
Footprints, feeding marks and nests can also become fossils; they are called trace fossils.

teile.einleitung: Stress is the reaction of body and mind to demands or threats. Before an exam, during an argument or when a dog suddenly barks, the body switches into a state of alarm. A little stress can spur you on, but too much stress over a long time makes you ill.
wichtigste: Positive stress that spurs you on is called eustress.
During acute stress, the heartbeat speeds up.
The adrenal glands release stress hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol.
During stress, the sympathetic nervous system, part of the nervous system, is activated.
The quick emergency reaction to a threat is called the fight-or-flight response.
According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, performance is usually best at a medium level of arousal.
If stress lasts a long time, according to Selye the final phase is exhaustion.
Regular exercise has been shown to help reduce stress.

abschnitte.text: Stress is a reaction to **stressors**, that is, to things that challenge or threaten us. This can be an exam, noise, time pressure, an argument or a dangerous situation. Positive stress that spurs you on is called **eustress**, and stress that weighs you down is called **distress**. Whether something feels like stress also depends on whether you feel up to the task.

When there is danger, the brain activates the **sympathetic nervous system**, part of the nervous system. The **adrenal glands** release stress hormones, first adrenaline and a little later cortisol. The heartbeat speeds up, you breathe faster, and the muscles get a better blood supply. This emergency reaction is called the **fight-or-flight response**, because it made our ancestors ready to fight or to run away.

The American physiologist Walter Cannon described the fight-or-flight response at the beginning of the 20th century. The Vienna-born researcher **Hans Selye** made the term stress well known from the 1930s onwards. He described the **general adaptation syndrome** with three phases: alarm reaction, resistance and exhaustion. If the stress lasts a long time, your strength is used up in the end.

According to the **Yerkes-Dodson law**, performance is usually best at a medium level of arousal. People who are not tense at all are often unfocused, while those who are too nervous make mistakes or have a blackout. A little stage fright before a talk can therefore even help. The law was described in 1908 by two American psychologists.

Short-term stress is normal and usually harmless. But if it lasts for weeks or months, it can lead to sleep problems, headaches or tummy aches and frequent colds. Lack of motivation, irritability and problems concentrating can also be warning signs. With very strong long-term stress, people sometimes speak of **burnout**, a state of complete exhaustion.

**Regular exercise** has been shown to help break down stress hormones. Enough sleep, breaks without screens, calm breathing and time with friends also do you good. Big tasks are easier to manage if you split them into small steps. If you are worried or do not know what to do, in Switzerland you can call Pro Juventute free of charge on 147, day and night.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that causes stress, for example noise or time pressure.
Positive stress that spurs you on.
Negative stress that weighs you down.
A hormone that gets the body ready for an emergency within seconds.
The part of the nervous system that activates the body during stress.

gewusst: The word stress originally comes from engineering, where it meant load or strain on a material.
The adrenal glands sit like little caps on top of the kidneys.
Animals have stress too, for example zebras fleeing from a lion, but their bodies usually calm down again quickly afterwards.

teile.einleitung: Swissuniversities is the rectors' conference of Swiss higher education institutions. Here the heads of universities, universities of applied sciences and universities of teacher education work together. The organisation represents the institutions to politicians and the public.
wichtigste: Swissuniversities is the rectors' conference of Swiss higher education institutions.
It has existed in its current form since 2015.
It is based on the Higher Education Act, HEdA for short.
Its chambers represent universities, universities of applied sciences and universities of teacher education.
Swissuniversities is based in Bern.
Among other things, it provides information about admission with foreign qualifications.
The highest political body in higher education is the Swiss Conference of Higher Education.

abschnitte.text: Swissuniversities is the joint **rectors' conference** of Swiss higher education institutions. A rector heads a university, in a similar way to how a head teacher runs a school. In Swissuniversities the rectors discuss common questions and speak with one voice. The organisation is based in **Bern**.

Swissuniversities has existed in its current form since **2015**. Before that, each type of institution had its own rectors' conference. The basis for the merger is the **Higher Education Act** (in German HFKG). This law sets out how the Confederation and the cantons jointly steer and fund higher education.

Swissuniversities is divided into three **chambers**. The first represents the universities, that is, the cantonal universities and the two Federal Institutes of Technology in Zurich and Lausanne. The second represents the **universities of applied sciences**, which offer practical training, for example in engineering, business or design. The third represents the **universities of teacher education**, where teachers are trained.

Swissuniversities coordinates questions about studies, teaching and research between the institutions. For example, it informs people from abroad who want to study about **admission** with foreign qualifications. It also represents Swiss higher education institutions in international networks. It works closely with the **Swiss Conference of Higher Education**, the highest political body of the Confederation and cantons in the field of higher education.

abschnitte.titel: Universities in all parts of the country
abschnitte.text: Switzerland has higher education institutions in all its language regions. The **Università della Svizzera italiana** in Lugano is the country's only Italian-speaking university. In Fribourg, students study bilingually in German and French. This diversity is typical of Switzerland and is represented jointly in Swissuniversities.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place of study after the Matura or vocational Matura, where people study and do research.
The person who heads a university.
A higher education institution with practical training, for example in engineering, business or health.
A higher education institution where future teachers are trained.

gewusst: The name Swissuniversities is usually written in lower case, that is, “swissuniversities”.
The University of Fribourg is one of the few universities in Europe where you can complete a whole degree bilingually.

teile.einleitung: The bee dance is the way honeybees show each other where there is food. To do this they perform special dances on the honeycombs in the dark hive. This amazing language was decoded by the researcher Karl von Frisch.
wichtigste: Honeybees dance to show other bees where there is food.
They dance on the honeycombs in the hive.
If the food is very close, they perform the round dance.
If the food is far away, they perform the waggle dance.
In the waggle dance, the bees use the sun to orient themselves.
From the scent that is brought back, the other bees recognise the type of flower.
Karl von Frisch decoded the bee dance and was awarded the Nobel Prize for it.

abschnitte.text: When a **forager bee** has found a good source of food, it flies back to the hive. There it performs a particular dance on the upright **honeycombs**. Other bees follow close behind it and feel its movements, because it is dark in the hive. In this way they learn in which direction and how far they have to fly.

If the food is very close to the hive, the bee performs the **round dance**. It runs in small circles, alternately to the left and to the right. This dance only says: “There is food very close by; search the surrounding area.” The round dance does not give an exact direction.

If the food is further away, the bee performs the **waggle dance**, which looks like a figure of eight. In the middle it runs straight ahead, waggling its abdomen strongly. The direction of this run shows the angle between the **sun** and the source of food: if it runs straight upwards, the food is exactly in the direction of the sun. The longer the bee waggles, the further away the destination is.

From the **scent** that the dancer brings back from the flowers, the other bees can smell which flowers they have to look for. The dancer often hands out samples of nectar too. The better the source of food, the more lively and longer it dances. In this way the most bees fly to the best flowers.

The Austrian researcher **Karl von Frisch** studied bees for decades using little food dishes and marked bees. He worked in Munich and Graz, among other places. For his discoveries he received the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine in 1973, together with Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen. His work showed that even insects communicate with each other with amazing precision.

begriffe.erklaerung: The movements with which honeybees tell other bees about sources of food.
A wall of six-sided wax cells in the beehive.
A dance in small circles that shows food nearby.
A figure-of-eight dance with waggling that shows the direction and distance of food.

gewusst: Bees can locate the sun even behind clouds, because they can see polarised light.
A waggle dance can show feeding places that are several kilometres away from the hive.
When dancing, bees even take into account that the sun moves on over the course of the day.

teile.einleitung: An observatory is a building from which people use telescopes to observe stars, planets and other celestial bodies. Some are used for research, others are public observatories that anyone who is interested can visit.
wichtigste: In an observatory you observe stars and planets.
The most important instrument is the telescope.
At the top of the dome, a slit opens for the telescope.
The best time to visit an observatory is on a clear night.
Many observatories are far away from towns, because it is darker there.
The Urania observatory stands right in the middle of the city of Zurich.
With a telescope you can see the craters on the Moon and the rings of Saturn.

abschnitte.text: An observatory, called **“Sternwarte”** or “Observatorium” in German, is a place for observing the sky. Its heart is a large **telescope**, which collects much more light than our eyes. With it you can see faint stars, planets, star clusters and distant galaxies. Research observatories mainly take measurements and photos, while public observatories show the sky to all visitors.

Many observatories have a round **dome** that can be turned. At the top, a slit opens through which the telescope looks at the sky. Because the Earth rotates, the stars move across the sky, so the telescope has to follow them. The dome protects the delicate instrument from rain, wind and dust.

The best time to observe is on a clear night without a moon. The light from street lamps and houses brightens the sky; this is called **light pollution**. That is why large observatories are usually far away from towns, often on high mountains where the air is dry and calm. Famous examples are the observatories in the Atacama Desert in Chile and on Mauna Kea in Hawaii.

Even with a small telescope you can make out the **craters** on the Moon. With the planet **Saturn** you can see its rings, and with Jupiter four bright moons. The star closest to the Earth is the Sun, and you must never look at it through a telescope without a special filter. Otherwise you could go blind immediately.

The **Urania** in Zurich is an observatory right in the middle of the city and was opened in 1907. Many places in Switzerland have public observatories, which are run by clubs and regularly offer public evenings. On the Jungfraujoch and the Gornergrat, research is carried out at high altitude. The University of Geneva runs an observatory whose researchers discovered the first planet orbiting a Sun-like star in 1995.

begriffe.erklaerung: An instrument that collects light and shows distant things enlarged.
A building or place for observing the sky; in German also “Sternwarte”.
Artificial light that brightens the night sky and makes stars invisible.
An observatory that is meant for the general public.

gewusst: Large telescopes are so sensitive that they could detect the light of a candle on the Moon.
Some observatories do not observe with light but with radio waves; they are called radio telescopes.

teile.einleitung: A symbiosis is when two different species live together and both benefit. The term comes from Greek and means “living together”. Symbioses exist everywhere in nature, in the forest, in the sea and even in our own tummies.
wichtigste: In a symbiosis, two species live together for their mutual benefit.
Mycorrhiza is a symbiosis between fungi and the roots of many trees.
Nodule bacteria supply legumes such as peas with nitrogen from the air.
Clownfish and sea anemones protect each other.
Cleaner fish free large fish from skin parasites.
Bacteria in the gut of cows break down hard-to-digest cellulose.
If only one species benefits without harming the other, it is called commensalism.

abschnitte.text: In a **symbiosis**, two different species live closely together and help each other. Each partner gives something and gets something back, for example food, protection or a home. The term was used by the German researcher Heinrich Anton de Bary in 1879. Some partners can no longer survive without each other at all.

Not every way of living together benefits both sides. In **commensalism**, one species benefits and the other has neither an advantage nor a disadvantage, like birds that nest in a tree. In **parasitism**, one has an advantage and the other is harmed, for example by a tick bite. So symbiosis is the friendliest form of living together.

Many trees such as spruces, beeches or larches live together with fungi; this is called **mycorrhiza**. The fungal threads wrap around the roots and supply the tree with water and mineral salts. In return the fungus gets sugar, which the tree makes using sunlight. Legumes such as peas, beans and clover house **nodule bacteria**, which supply them with nitrogen from the air.

The **clownfish** lives among the poisonous tentacles of a sea anemone, which protects it from enemies. In return it chases away fish that want to nibble the anemone. Small **cleaner fish** free large fish from skin parasites and get their food that way. Bees and flowers are partners too: the bee gets nectar, and the flower is pollinated so that fruit can form.

Cows eat a lot of grass, but they cannot digest the tough **cellulose** in it themselves. This work is done by tiny bacteria in their rumen, part of the stomach. Trillions of useful bacteria also live in the human gut; they are called the **gut flora**. They help with digestion and protect against pathogens.

A special symbiosis is found in **lichens**, which consist of a fungus and an alga. The fungus provides support and stores water, while the alga makes food using sunlight. Together, lichens can grow on bare rocks, tree bark or walls. In the Swiss Alps they often cover whole stones with yellow, grey or orange patches.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two species living together in a way that benefits both.
One species benefits, the other has neither an advantage nor a disadvantage.
One species lives at the expense of another and harms it.
The partnership between fungi and the roots of plants.
A tough substance in the walls of plant cells that is hard to digest.

gewusst: Many edible mushrooms such as the penny bun only grow where their partner tree stands.
Lichens often grow only a few millimetres a year and can become very old.
Corals live together with tiny algae that give them their bright colours and part of their food.

teile.einleitung: Stratigraphy is the study of layers in the ground and in rock. Archaeologists and geologists read these layers like the pages of a book to find out what happened first and what happened later.
wichtigste: Stratigraphy deals with the sequence of layers of soil and rock.
The Latin word stratum means covering or layer.
In 1669 Nicolaus Steno formulated the law of superposition.
Stratigraphy provides a relative dating.
Archaeologists show the sequence of layers in a Harris matrix.
A cultural layer contains traces of human activity.
In the Middle East, mounds made of many settlement layers are called tells.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin **stratum**, covering or layer, and the Greek graphein, to write. Stratigraphy studies how layers lie on top of one another in the ground. In geology it is about rock layers that formed over millions of years. In **archaeology** it is about layers that people left behind with rubbish, buildings and fires.

In 1669 the Danish naturalist **Nicolaus Steno** formulated the law of superposition. It states that in undisturbed layers, the lower ones are older than the upper ones. You can imagine a pile of newspapers onto which a new one is put every day. At the very bottom is the oldest newspaper, at the very top the newest. Steno is therefore regarded as one of the founders of geology.

Stratigraphy tells you what is older and what is younger, but not exactly how old. This is called **relative dating**. If you find a coin in a layer that was minted in AD 150, the layer was formed in the year 150 at the earliest. A pit that cuts through three layers is younger than these layers. For exact dates you need further methods such as radiocarbon dating or the tree rings of wood.

During an excavation, archaeologists carefully remove one layer after another and record everything. Each layer, pit or wall is given a number. They show the sequence in a diagram, the **Harris matrix**, which the archaeologist Edward Harris developed in the 1970s. This shows at a glance what came into being before and after something else.

A **cultural layer** contains traces of human activity such as shards, bones, ash or remains of wood. In Switzerland, such layers are found for example at the pile-dwelling settlements on lake shores, which are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In the Middle East, towns grew higher and higher on their own ruins over thousands of years. This created mounds made of many settlement layers, which are called **tells**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A deposit of earth, rock or rubbish that has settled over another one.
Working out what is older and what is younger, without an exact date.
A layer of soil with traces of people, such as shards or ash.
A mound that has formed from many settlements lying on top of one another.

gewusst: In the walls of the Grand Canyon in the USA, you can read almost two billion years of Earth's history in the layers.
Nicolaus Steno was not only a naturalist; he later also became a bishop.

teile.einleitung: A pond is a small, fairly shallow body of still water that has often been made by people. Despite its small size, it is a paradise for animals and plants, from frogs and newts to dragonflies and water lilies. If you sit quietly on the bank, you can discover a lot there.
wichtigste: A pond is smaller and shallower than a lake.
Many ponds were made by people, for example as fish ponds, fire ponds or garden ponds.
Reeds and other tall plants often grow on the bank, and water lilies float on the water.
Tadpoles turn into frogs, and young dragonflies first live in the water.
Pond skaters can walk over the water without sinking.
In spring newts come to the pond, and mallards often swim on it.
When it is very cold, a pond freezes over on top in winter.

abschnitte.text: A pond is a body of **still water**, that is, water without a strong current. It is smaller and shallower than a lake, often only one to two metres deep. Because the light usually reaches the bottom, plants can grow almost everywhere. Ponds are often made by people, while small natural bodies of still water are often called **“Weiher”** in German. In everyday language, though, both words are used in a similar way.

abschnitte.titel: Plants by and in the water
abschnitte.text: On the bank grow tall plants such as **reeds**, bulrushes and rushes. Further out, the large round leaves of the **water lily** float on the surface. Underwater grow plants such as Canadian waterweed, which release oxygen into the water. The plants form different zones, from the damp bank to the deeper water.

In spring, frogs and toads lay their spawn in the pond. **Tadpoles** hatch from it; at first they breathe with gills, and later they turn into little frogs. **Newts** with their long tails also come into the water in spring. Young dragonflies, the larvae, live in the pond for one to several years and hunt there before they emerge as flying dragonflies. Mallards swim on the water, and fish such as carp or sunbleak live in it.

The **pond skater** has fine, water-repellent hairs on its legs. Because of this, the **surface tension** of the water carries it, and it can dart around on it. Whirligig beetles spin in fast circles on the surface. The backswimmer, as its name says, swims on its back just below the surface of the water.

In summer the shallow water can get warm, and algae sometimes grow strongly. In winter, when it is very cold, the pond freezes over on top. Because ice is lighter than water, it floats on top, and underneath the water stays liquid at about four degrees. In this way fish and many animals can spend the winter at the bottom. Frogs and newts often spend the winter in the mud or on land under leaves.

In Switzerland, many wetlands and small bodies of water disappeared in the last century because land was drained. That is why newly made **ponds** are very important for amphibians such as the tree frog or the great crested newt. Nature conservation organisations and municipalities therefore create new ponds. Even a natural garden pond without fish can help frogs and dragonflies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A body of water in which the water hardly flows, for example a pond or lake.
The larva of a frog or toad, which lives in the water.
The eggs of frogs, toads or fish in the water.
A force that holds the surface of water together like a thin skin.
An animal such as a frog or newt that lives in water and on land.

gewusst: A pond skater can feel through the tiny ripples on the surface when an insect has fallen into the water.
Dragonfly larvae catch their prey with a catching mask that shoots out lightning fast.
Fish in garden ponds often eat the spawn and tadpoles of frogs.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Light Source, SLS for short, is a large research facility at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen in the canton of Aargau. In a ring, electrons race round almost at the speed of light and produce extremely bright X-ray light as they do so. With this light, researchers can look into the tiniest structures, right down to individual atoms.
wichtigste: The SLS is located at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen in the canton of Aargau and started operating in 2001.
Its storage ring has a circumference of about 290 metres.
Synchrotron radiation is produced when fast electrons are deflected by magnets.
Undulators with many magnets of alternating polarity produce especially bright light.
The light is led to the measuring stations through beamlines.
There is an ultra-high vacuum in the storage ring, so that the electrons do not collide with gas molecules.
With the upgrade project SLS 2.0, the facility received a new storage ring from 2023 with much more brilliant X-ray light.

abschnitte.text: The SLS stands on the site of the **Paul Scherrer Institute** on the River Aare, between Brugg and Zurzach. The round building is easy to recognise from outside and looks like a giant UFO. The PSI is Switzerland's largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering. Every year researchers from many countries come here to carry out their experiments.

First, electrons are produced and brought to high energy in a **linear accelerator** and a pre-accelerator. Then they circle in the **storage ring**, where strong magnets keep them on their path. Every time the electrons are steered round a bend, they give off light, the synchrotron radiation. Until the rebuild in 2023, the electrons had an energy of 2.4 gigaelectronvolts (GeV). Because hardly anything may disturb them, there is an **ultra-high vacuum** in the ring.

An **undulator** consists of many small magnets with alternating polarity. This makes the electrons fly back and forth as if on a slalom course, and they send out especially focused, bright light. This light is led through **beamlines** to the experimental stations around the ring. Each beamline specialises in certain kinds of study, for example X-ray images, spectroscopy or crystal measurements.

The SLS is used particularly often to **determine the structure of proteins**. In this way researchers from universities and the pharmaceutical industry find out how proteins are built and where a medicine can dock. New materials for batteries, computer chips or solar cells are also studied here. The X-ray light can even be used to look inside fossils and works of art without damaging them.

After more than 20 years of operation, the facility was modernised. In autumn 2023 it was switched off, and as part of **SLS 2.0** a completely new storage ring was installed. The electrons now circle at about 2.7 GeV, and the X-ray light is many times brighter and more finely focused. In 2025 the renewed facility started operating again.

begriffe.erklaerung: Very bright light that is produced when fast electrons are steered onto a curved path.
A ring-shaped tube in which electrons fly round and round for hours.
A row of magnets that makes electrons swing in a slalom and so produces especially bright light.
A space from which almost all the air has been removed.
A path with mirrors and instruments that leads the light from the ring to an experiment.

gewusst: The electrons in the SLS go round the ring about a million times a second.
The X-ray light of the SLS is billions of times brighter than that of an X-ray machine at the doctor's.
At the PSI there is a second large X-ray facility, SwissFEL, which produces extremely short flashes of light.

teile.einleitung: Tadeus Reichstein was a Swiss chemist who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1950. He was one of the first to produce vitamin C artificially, and he researched hormones that are still important in medicine today. He was born in Poland in 1897 and died in Basel in 1996 at the age of 99.
wichtigste: Tadeus Reichstein lived from 1897 to 1996 and reached the age of 99.
In 1933 he succeeded in producing vitamin C artificially.
He studied hormones of the adrenal cortex, which belong to the steroids.
The hormone cortisone was soon used against rheumatoid arthritis.
In 1950 he received the Nobel Prize together with Edward Kendall and Philip Hench.
From 1938 he was professor of pharmaceutical chemistry at the University of Basel.
In old age he studied ferns intensively.

abschnitte.text: Tadeus Reichstein was born on 20 July 1897 in Włocławek in what is now Poland. His family moved to Switzerland, and he grew up in Zurich. There he studied chemistry at **ETH Zurich** and completed a doctorate. Later he became a Swiss citizen.

In 1933 Reichstein succeeded in producing **vitamin C** in the laboratory, independently of its occurrence in fruit. His method, the Reichstein synthesis, was suitable for large quantities. The Basel company Roche used it to produce vitamin C cheaply. Vitamin C is important for the body's defences, and a lack of it can cause the disease scurvy.

From the 1930s, Reichstein studied the **adrenal cortex**, part of a small gland above the kidney. From it he isolated numerous hormones, all of which belong to the class of substances called **steroids**. One of them was **cortisone**, which soon proved to be an effective remedy for rheumatoid arthritis and inflammation. Today cortisone preparations are used, for example, for allergies, asthma and skin diseases.

For his research on the hormones of the adrenal cortex, Reichstein received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1950. He shared it with the US researchers Edward Kendall and Philip Hench. From 1938 he was professor of pharmaceutical chemistry at the **University of Basel**. Later he headed the Institute of Organic Chemistry there.

After his retirement Reichstein continued his research, now mainly on **ferns**. He studied their substances and the cell nuclei of many species of fern. He went on publishing scientific papers into old age. He died in Basel on 1 August 1996.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that the body needs in small amounts and usually takes in with food.
A messenger substance in the body that controls important processes.
A group of chemical substances with a similar structure, which includes many hormones.
Making a substance in the laboratory from simpler substances.

gewusst: Reichstein lived through almost the whole of the 20th century; he reached the age of 99.
As well as chemistry, Reichstein was interested in plants all his life, especially ferns.
His method of producing vitamin C was used in industry around the world for decades.

teile.einleitung: SwissFEL is a huge research facility at the Paul Scherrer Institute in the canton of Aargau. It produces extremely short and bright X-ray flashes with which very fast processes in molecules can be observed. You can think of it as a super-fast camera for the tiniest world.
wichtigste: SwissFEL is located at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen in the canton of Aargau.
The facility was officially inaugurated in 2016.
It is about 740 metres long in total.
The electrons are accelerated in a linear accelerator.
SwissFEL produces at most 100 X-ray pulses per second.
The pulses last only a few to several dozen femtoseconds.
The two beamlines are called Aramis and Athos.
The facility cost about 275 million francs.

abschnitte.text: SwissFEL is a **free-electron laser** that produces X-ray light. The abbreviation FEL stands for Free Electron Laser. The facility is located at the **Paul Scherrer Institute** in Villigen in the canton of Aargau, Switzerland's largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering. It was officially inaugurated in 2016 and cost about 275 million francs.

First, electrons are brought almost to the speed of light in a straight **linear accelerator**. Then they fly through long rows of magnets called **undulators**. The magnets force the electrons onto a wavy path, and as they move they send out X-ray light. This light builds up into an extremely bright, laser-like flash.

The whole facility is about **740 metres** long, roughly as long as seven football pitches one after another. It is housed in a long, low building that is partly hidden in the forest floor. There are two beamlines with names from a famous novel: **Aramis** for hard and **Athos** for soft X-rays. Soft X-rays have less energy than hard ones.

The X-ray pulses last only a few to several dozen **femtoseconds**. A femtosecond is one quadrillionth of a second. SwissFEL can produce at most 100 such pulses per second. Because the flashes are so short, they can be used like a camera to capture individual moments of **molecular processes**.

With SwissFEL, researchers observe how chemical reactions take place or how proteins change their shape. This helps, for example, in developing new **medicines**. New materials for electronics or solar cells are also studied. There are only a few such **X-ray lasers** in the world, so researchers come to Villigen from many countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible, high-energy light that can pass through many substances.
A straight facility in which tiny particles such as electrons are made very fast.
A row of magnets that forces electrons onto a wavy path so that they send out light.
An unimaginably short period of time: one quadrillionth of a second.

gewusst: In one femtosecond, even light travels only about a third of a thousandth of a millimetre.
The names Aramis and Athos come from two characters in the novel “The Three Musketeers”.
Because the facility is in such demand, researchers have to apply with their ideas and are given only a few days of measuring time.

teile.einleitung: In microbiology, sterilisation means completely freeing objects, liquids or rooms of all living microorganisms. It is essential in hospitals, in laboratories and in the food industry, so that no germs cause diseases.
wichtigste: Sterilisation kills all microorganisms, including tough spores.
Disinfection, by contrast, only kills most pathogens.
In its standard programme an autoclave usually works at 121 °C.
Because of the increased pressure, the steam becomes hotter than 100 °C.
Bacterial endospores are especially resistant to heat.
Heat-sensitive solutions are filtered with filters of about 0.2 micrometres.
Many disposable syringes are sterilised with gamma radiation.

abschnitte.text: Sterile means free of germs, so without any living bacteria, fungi or viruses. In **sterilisation**, all microorganisms are killed, including their tough resting forms. **Disinfection**, on the other hand, only kills most pathogens, for example when you disinfect your hands. Sterile instruments are needed for operations, injections and a lot of laboratory work.

The most important device is the **autoclave**, a kind of large pressure cooker. Inside it, steam is heated under increased pressure so that it becomes hotter than 100 °C. In its standard programme an autoclave usually works at 121 °C for about 15 to 20 minutes. The hot steam gets deep into the objects and reliably kills the germs. The autoclave was invented around 1879 by Charles Chamberland, a colleague of Louis Pasteur.

Some bacteria form **endospores**, which are especially tough resting forms. They survive boiling water, dryness and many chemicals. That is why pasteurisation, as used for milk, does not count as sterilisation, because heat-resistant germs and spores survive it. How quickly germs die is described by the **D-value**, the time in which 90 per cent of the germs are killed at a certain temperature. With 1 million spores and a D-value of 2 minutes, statistically 100 spores are still left after 8 minutes.

Not everything can cope with steam, so there are other methods. Glass and metal can be sterilised in dry hot air at about 180 °C. Heat-sensitive liquids such as some medicines are pushed through fine **filters** with pores of about 0.2 micrometres, which hold back bacteria. Many disposable medical products such as syringes are sterilised in the factory with **gamma radiation**, often when they are already packed.

In the past, many people died of infections after operations. Only in the 19th century did researchers such as Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister realise that germs cause diseases. Since then, sterilising instruments has been one of the most important rules in hospitals. Tins of food are also heated so that no dangerous bacteria can multiply inside them.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny living things such as bacteria and fungi that you can only see under a microscope.
A device that makes objects free of germs using hot steam under pressure.
A very tough resting form of some bacteria.
Killing most pathogens, but not necessarily all germs.

gewusst: A pressure cooker in the kitchen works on the same principle as an autoclave.
Some bacterial spores can survive for decades or even longer and then become active again.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Science Center Technorama in Winterthur is a science centre where you can experience natural sciences with your own hands. Instead of just looking at things, you can try out hundreds of experiments yourself. It is one of the largest science centres in Switzerland and a popular destination for school classes and families.
wichtigste: The Technorama is in Winterthur in the canton of Zurich.
It is a science centre, not a traditional museum.
You are allowed to try out the exhibits yourself.
You can experiment with light, magnets, water and much more.
It is meant above all for marvelling and discovering.
A glass prism shows that white light is made of the colours of the rainbow.

abschnitte.text: The **Technorama** is a **science centre** in Winterthur in the canton of Zurich. In a science centre you do not learn by reading signs but by trying things out yourself. The Technorama started as a technology museum and later became a house of experiments. Today its official name is Swiss Science Center Technorama.

In the section about light you can experiment with mirrors, lenses and prisms. A **glass prism** splits white light into the colours of the rainbow. With a mirror you explore how light is **reflected** and why the mirror image appears the wrong way round. Optical illusions show how easily our brain can be tricked.

With a **magnet** you can try out which things are attracted, for example an iron nail. Other experiments show invisible magnetic fields with iron filings. In a show you experience how high electrical **voltage** creates flashes of lightning. It is also explained why you need to be careful of lightning.

Many experiments show how water and air move. You can create whirls, watch waves or make currents visible. Other stations explain gravity, balance and chance. Outside in the park there are also large experiments, for example with **water** and sound.

For school classes there are **workshops** and laboratories in which children and young people do their own research. Many classes from all over Switzerland visit the Technorama on a school trip. The aim is to awaken curiosity and enjoyment of science and technology. If you discover something yourself, you often understand it and remember it better.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place where you discover natural sciences by experimenting yourself.
A piece of glass that splits white light into its colours.
An object that attracts things made of iron.
A test in which you try something out and observe it.

gewusst: There are almost no “Do not touch” signs in the Technorama, because touching is expressly encouraged.
White light is actually a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow.
A rainbow forms because raindrops split sunlight like little prisms.

teile.einleitung: A streamlined shape is round at the front and narrow at the back, which is why it glides especially easily through air or water. Fish, penguins and birds have it naturally. Engineers build cars, trains and aeroplanes on this model so that they use less energy.
wichtigste: A streamlined shape is round at the front and narrow at the back.
The teardrop shape is considered especially good for gliding through air.
Vehicles with a streamlined shape use less energy.
When cycling fast, it is mainly air resistance that slows you down.
Racing cyclists crouch low over the handlebars so that less air slows them down.
Penguins and tuna swim very fast thanks to their streamlined shape.
In a wind tunnel, engineers test how strongly a car is slowed down by the wind.

abschnitte.text: When something moves through air or water, it constantly has to push it aside. This slows it down; this is called **drag**, or in air **air resistance**. A streamlined shape is round at the front and gets narrower towards the back, so that the air or water can flow smoothly around it. The **teardrop shape** is considered especially good.

With an angular shape, the flow breaks away and forms eddies at the back. These eddies, as it were, suck at the object and slow it down a lot. With a streamlined shape, the flow stays close to the body for longer and hardly forms any eddies. How good a shape is, is described by the **drag coefficient**: the smaller it is, the less resistance.

The **penguin** cannot fly, but thanks to its streamlined body it swims very fast underwater. The **tuna**, with its spindle-shaped body, is also a fast swimmer. Dolphins, trout and seals have similar shapes. Birds fold in their wings when diving so that they are slowed down less.

Cars, trains and aeroplanes are often built with a streamlined shape, because then they use **less energy**. In a **wind tunnel**, air is blown at a car or a model and engineers measure how strongly it is slowed down. A Japanese high-speed train was given a long nose modelled on the beak of the kingfisher, so that it does not make a loud bang when entering tunnels. Racing cars are also tested in wind tunnels for a long time, for example by the Sauber Formula 1 team in Hinwil in the canton of Zurich.

When cycling fast, it is mainly **air resistance** that slows you down, and it grows strongly with speed. That is why racing cyclists crouch low over the handlebars so that less air slows them down. Time trial riders wear smooth suits and teardrop-shaped helmets. Ski racers also go into a low crouch in the downhill, which is called the egg.

begriffe.erklaerung: The braking force that air exerts on something that is moving.
A facility in which air is blown against vehicles or models to measure the resistance.
A number that shows how streamlined a shape is; in German it is called the “cw-Wert”.
A swirling flow that forms behind angular shapes.

gewusst: If you double the speed, the air resistance becomes about four times as large.
A drop falling from a tap actually has a rather round shape and not the typical teardrop shape.
The kingfisher dives head first into the water with hardly any splash.

teile.einleitung: A stopwatch is a watch that you use to measure how long something takes. You start it at the press of a button and stop it again when something is over. Whether in a race during PE, when boiling eggs or in a ski race: stopwatches help to measure time precisely.
wichtigste: With a stopwatch you measure how long something takes.
In a race, you press the stopwatch for the first time at the start.
The display 01:30 means one minute and 30 seconds when the minutes are shown first.
The “Reset” button sets the time back to zero.
Whoever needs less time for the same distance is faster.
In ski races, time is measured to the hundredth of a second.
Today a stopwatch is often found in your mobile phone.

abschnitte.text: A stopwatch does not show the time of day, but how **long** something lasts. At the start you press a button and the watch begins to count. At the finish you press again and the time stops. With the **Reset** button you set the time back to zero.

Many stopwatches show minutes, seconds and hundredths of a second. If the minutes are shown first, 01:30 means one minute and 30 seconds, so 90 seconds. One second has 100 **hundredths of a second**. So at 12.45 seconds, 12 whole seconds and 45 hundredths have passed.

Lina runs a distance in 12 seconds, Tim the same distance in 15 seconds. Lina is faster, because she needs **less time**. If Lea needs 20 seconds for one lap, three laps at the same speed take 60 seconds, so exactly one minute. Many stopwatches have a button for **split times**, so that you can see each lap separately.

In ski races, time is measured to the **hundredth of a second**, and often a tiny difference decides who wins.
