There, nobody presses a button; instead the time is measured electronically with **light barriers** and start gates. A person, with a reaction time of about two tenths of a second, would measure too inaccurately. Swiss watch companies such as Omega and Longines have long been official timekeepers at big sporting events, for example at the Olympic Games.

abschnitte.titel: From pocket watch to mobile phone
abschnitte.text: The first watches for timing were built at the beginning of the 19th century. Mechanical stopwatches have clockwork with a spring and a large hand that moves over a dial. Later came **digital stopwatches** with a number display, which work with a vibrating quartz crystal. Today there is a stopwatch in almost every **mobile phone** and in many sports watches.

Stopwatches are not only used in sport. In the kitchen a timer helps to make sure eggs do not get too hard. In lessons you might measure, for example, how long a pendulum takes for one swing. In scientific experiments, too, accurate timing is often crucial.

begriffe.erklaerung: The length of time between the beginning and the end of something.
The hundredth part of a second.
The time that has passed up to a certain point during a run.
A beam of light that triggers a time measurement when it is interrupted.
A wristwatch with a built-in stopwatch function.

gewusst: In a photo finish, a picture of the finish line decides who arrived first.
A watch with a stopwatch function is called a chronograph, after the Greek words for “time” and “write”.
In swimming pools, athletes stop their own time by touching a touch pad at the finish.

teile.einleitung: Svante Pääbo is a Swedish researcher who studies ancient DNA from bones and mummies. With his team, he was the first to decode large parts of the genetic material of the Neanderthal. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2022.
wichtigste: Svante Pääbo was born in 1955 in Stockholm, Sweden.
He is regarded as a co-founder of palaeogenetics, the study of ancient genetic material.
As early as the 1980s he obtained DNA from an Egyptian mummy.
His team was the first to decode large parts of the Neanderthal genome.
He does research at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig.
In 2022 he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
His father Sune Bergström had also received a Nobel Prize.

abschnitte.text: Svante Pääbo was born in **Stockholm** in 1955. His mother was a chemist from Estonia, and his father was the Swedish biochemist **Sune Bergström**. At Uppsala University, Pääbo first studied Egyptology and then medicine. The link between ancient cultures and modern biology shaped his whole career.

Even as a young researcher, Pääbo wondered whether genetic material was still preserved in ancient bodies. In the 1980s he succeeded in obtaining DNA from an **Egyptian mummy**. This was a sensation, because after death DNA slowly breaks down into tiny pieces. This gave rise to a new field of research, **palaeogenetics**.

The Neanderthal lived in Europe and western Asia from about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. Pääbo's team examined bone remains and put the genetic material together like a huge puzzle. In 2010 they published a first draft of the **Neanderthal genome**. It showed that many people today outside Africa carry a small share of Neanderthal genetic material.

The team also obtained DNA from a tiny finger bone from the **Denisova Cave** in Siberia. The genetic material matched neither modern humans nor Neanderthals. In this way a previously unknown form of human was discovered, the **Denisovan**. It was the first time that a form of human had been identified only through its genetic material.

The biggest difficulty with ancient DNA is **contamination** with modern DNA. Even a flake of skin or a breath from a researcher can spoil a sample. That is why Pääbo's team works in especially clean clean rooms with protective suits and masks. Today experts from all over the world, including Switzerland, work according to these strict rules.

Since 1997 Pääbo has headed a department at the **Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology** in Leipzig. In 2022 he alone received the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine**. His father had already been awarded a Nobel Prize in the same category in 1982. Pääbo's research helps us understand what distinguishes modern humans from their extinct relatives.

begriffe.erklaerung: The building plan in every cell in which a living thing's hereditary information is stored.
All the DNA of a living thing, that is, all its hereditary information together.
The science that studies ancient genetic material from bones, teeth or mummies.
An extinct form of human that lived in Europe until about 40,000 years ago.
When foreign, modern DNA gets into an ancient sample and spoils the result.

gewusst: At first Pääbo did his mummy experiments secretly at night and at weekends, because they were not part of his actual studies.
The finger bone from which the Denisovan was discovered was smaller than a fingernail.
Father and son both received a Nobel Prize in the same category, which is very rare.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Supercomputing Centre, CSCS for short, is Switzerland's national centre for high-performance computers. It is located in Lugano in Ticino and belongs to ETH Zurich. Some of the fastest computers in Europe work here for science and weather forecasting.
wichtigste: The CSCS is located in Lugano in the canton of Ticino.
It belongs to ETH Zurich.
The computers are cooled with water from Lake Lugano.
Its long-serving supercomputer was called Piz Daint, after a mountain in the Grisons.
In 2024 the new Alps infrastructure, which replaces Piz Daint, was inaugurated.
MeteoSwiss calculates its weather models on CSCS computers.
Computing power is measured in FLOPS.

abschnitte.text: The CSCS was founded in 1991 and is part of **ETH Zurich**. Since 2012 it has been housed in a modern building in **Lugano**. Researchers from universities all over Switzerland can apply for computing time there. This means that not every university has to buy its own expensive giant computers.

A **supercomputer** consists of thousands of processors that work on one task at the same time. It is millions of times faster than an ordinary laptop. Its performance is measured in **FLOPS**, that is, calculations with decimal numbers per second. The **TOP500** ranking compares the fastest supercomputers in the world twice a year.

The best-known computer at the CSCS was called **Piz Daint**, named after a mountain in the canton of the Grisons. For many years it was one of the fastest computers in Europe. In 2024 the new research infrastructure **Alps** was inaugurated. It uses modern graphics processors and is particularly well suited to artificial intelligence and climate research.

Supercomputers get very hot when they compute, a bit like a laptop on your lap, only much more so. For this, the CSCS pumps cold water from the depths of **Lake Lugano** through a long pipe. The lake water absorbs the heat and then flows back. In this way the centre saves a lot of electricity for air conditioning and protects the **environment**.

**MeteoSwiss** has its weather models for Switzerland calculated on CSCS computers. Researchers there simulate, for example, the climate, earthquakes, new materials or processes in the human body. Training large AI models also needs enormous computing power. Such **simulations** would be far too slow on normal computers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge computer made of thousands of processors that calculates extremely fast.
The unit of computing power: how many calculations with decimal numbers are possible per second.
A ranking that compares the 500 fastest computers in the world twice a year.
A copy of a real process in the computer, for example of the weather.

gewusst: The water for cooling is taken from a depth of about 45 metres in Lake Lugano, where it is cool all year round.
A supercomputer like Alps fills a whole hall with many cupboard-sized computer racks.
For a weather forecast, the computer calculates the weather for millions of small cubes of air above Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A table is an arrangement of data in rows and columns. In this way a lot of information can be shown clearly and you can quickly look something up. We come across tables every day, from the school timetable to the train timetable.
wichtigste: A table arranges data in rows and columns.
The horizontal lines are called rows.
The vertical lines are called columns.
A single box is called a cell.
The first row usually contains the headings.
The school timetable is a table.
With tables you can easily compare and add up numbers.

abschnitte.text: A **table** is a grid of boxes in which you enter words or numbers. The horizontal lines are called **rows**, the vertical ones **columns**. Where a row and a column cross, there is a **cell**. Each cell holds exactly one piece of information.

At the very top, in the first row, there are usually the **headings**, also called the header row. They say what is in each column, for example “Name”, “Age” or “Favourite fruit”. Often the first column also has labels, such as the days of the week. So you know straight away where to find a particular piece of information.

A survey shows: apple 7 children, banana 5 children, pear 3 children. If you add them up, that is 7 plus 5 plus 3, so 15 children. If a weather table shows Monday 3 degrees and Tuesday 7 degrees, it was 4 degrees warmer on Tuesday. So tables help with **comparing** and **adding up**.

The **school timetable** shows the days of the week in columns and the lessons in rows. The SBB train timetable, the league table of a football league or the nutritional information on a packet are also tables. In maths there is the times table. In chemistry, the **periodic table** arranges all the elements in one big table.

On the computer you create tables with a **spreadsheet** program, for example Excel or LibreOffice Calc. There the computer can automatically add up numbers in the cells or calculate averages. With one click, the data can be turned into charts. As long as about 4000 years ago, people in Mesopotamia wrote tables of numbers on clay tablets.

begriffe.erklaerung: A horizontal line in a table.
A vertical line in a table.
A single box where a row and a column cross.
A computer program with which you create tables and calculate in them.

gewusst: The word table comes from the Latin “tabula”, meaning board or tablet.
The periodic table of the elements is one of the most famous tables in the world.
In a spreadsheet, a single table can have more than a million rows.

teile.einleitung: A straw man argument is a trick in discussions in which you distort the other person's opinion and then attack this false version. So you fight against a straw dummy instead of the real opponent. If you know the trick, you can argue more fairly and defend yourself better.
wichtigste: In a straw man argument, you refute a distorted version of the opposing position.
The image probably comes from a straw dummy, which is easy to defeat.
You can recognise a straw man when the opposing position is exaggerated.
A good counter-strategy is to repeat your own position precisely.
The opposite of a straw man is the steel man, in which you examine the strongest form of the opposing position.
The principle of charity requires you to interpret other people's statements as reasonably as possible.
The straw man argument is regarded as a fallacy.

abschnitte.text: A **straw man argument** is a fallacy in reasoning. Instead of responding to what someone really said, you present their opinion in an exaggerated or twisted way. Then you refute this weak version and pretend that you have refuted the real opinion. The name probably comes from a **straw dummy**, which is easy to knock over because it does not fight back.

A says: “We should build more cycle paths.” B replies: “So A wants to ban all cars!” That is a straw man, because A said nothing about banning cars. It is similar when a researcher suggests testing a medicine further and a critic says: “So she claims it cures everything!” The critic is building up an **exaggerated** claim that is easy to attack.

A warning sign is when someone sums up the opposing position in an **exaggerated** way or with words like “so” and “always”. Often a small suggestion is turned into an extreme demand. Sometimes someone only picks out the weakest point and ignores the good reasons. You should ask yourself: did the person really say that?

abschnitte.titel: What you can do about it
abschnitte.text: If someone answers with a straw man, it helps to repeat **your own position** calmly and precisely. You can also say in a friendly way: “That is not what I claimed; what I meant was this.” The other way round, you can ask whether you have understood someone correctly. That way the discussion stays on the actual topic.

The opposite of the straw man is the **steel man**. Here you present the opposing position in its strongest form before you examine it. This goes well with the **principle of charity**, which requires you to interpret other people's statements as reasonably as possible. People who discuss like this learn more and often end up being more convincing.

In the 19th century, the philosopher **Arthur Schopenhauer** already described similar tricks in his work on the art of being right. One of them consists of exaggerating and stretching the opponent's claim. You come across straw man arguments in discussions in the playground, on social media and in politics. In Switzerland, with its many popular votes, it is especially important to present arguments fairly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mistake in thinking in which a conclusion is not properly justified.
A reason that you use to support an opinion.
The strongest and fairest presentation of an opposing position.
Understanding other people's statements in a way that makes them as reasonable as possible.

gewusst: In German the fallacy is called “Strohmann-Argument”, and the steel man is called “Stahlmann”.
In the past, soldiers practised fighting on dummies made of straw, which of course put up no resistance.
Scarecrows are a kind of straw man too: they look like people but are harmless.

teile.einleitung: Technology transfer means that knowledge from research is turned into products and services. In this way an invention from a university laboratory is meant to find its way into everyday life. Switzerland is regarded as one of the most innovative countries in the world.
wichtigste: Technology transfer is the transfer of research knowledge into commercial use.
At ETH Zurich, the office ETH transfer takes care of patents, licences and spin-offs.
Switzerland Innovation is a network of innovation parks at several locations.
Innosuisse funds projects in which universities and companies work together.
The Technology Readiness Level scale describes the stage of development of a technology from 1 to 9.
The “Valley of Death” means the funding gap between research and the market.
A confidentiality agreement protects an invention before it has been registered.

abschnitte.text: In **technology transfer**, knowledge moves from universities and research institutes into companies. In this way an idea in the laboratory becomes, for example, a new medicine, a sensor or a piece of software. This can happen through **licences**, in which a company is allowed to use an invention and pays for it. Researchers also often found their own company, a so-called **spin-off**.

Every large university has a transfer office; at ETH Zurich it is called **ETH transfer**. It helps with registering patents, granting licences and supporting spin-offs. The Confederation's funding agency, **Innosuisse**, supports innovation projects by universities and companies. Typically the research partner receives the funding, while the company makes its own contribution.

**Switzerland Innovation** is a network of innovation parks at several locations in Switzerland. There, researchers, start-ups and large companies work close to one another. One location is, for example, near the Paul Scherrer Institute in Aargau, another in Dübendorf near Zurich. Being close together is meant to help ideas become products more quickly.

abschnitte.titel: From the laboratory to the market
abschnitte.text: How far a technology has been developed is described by the **Technology Readiness Level** scale from 1 to 9. Level 1 is just a basic principle on paper, level 9 a proven system in real use. Between research and market launch there is often a lack of money; this gap is called the **Valley of Death**. Many good ideas fail at exactly this point.

An invention can only be patented if it is new and has not yet been published. That is why the university and the company often first sign a **confidentiality agreement**, NDA for short. In the USA, the **Bayh-Dole Act** of 1980 allowed universities to hold patents on research funded by the state. This law is regarded as a milestone of technology transfer worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: A right that gives a person or company sole ownership of an invention for a certain time.
Permission to use a protected invention in return for payment.
A new company that grows out of a university or research institute.
A new idea that is actually put into practice and used.

gewusst: Switzerland has been in first place in the worldwide innovation ranking, the Global Innovation Index, for many years.
Dozens of new spin-off companies come out of ETH Zurich every year.
A patent usually lasts at most 20 years; after that anyone may use the invention.

teile.einleitung: Swissmedic is the Swiss authority that authorises and monitors medicines and medical devices. Before a new medicine may be sold in Switzerland, Swissmedic checks whether it is well made, safe and effective. In this way the authority protects the health of people and animals.
wichtigste: Swissmedic is the Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products, based in Bern.
The authority has been carrying out its tasks since 2002.
Its work is based on the Therapeutic Products Act.
Before authorisation, Swissmedic checks quality, safety and effectiveness.
Even after authorisation, Swissmedic evaluates reports of side effects.
As well as medicines, Swissmedic also monitors medical devices.
Swissmedic is a federal public-law institution assigned to the Department of Home Affairs.

abschnitte.text: Swissmedic is the **Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products**, that is, the national supervisory authority for therapeutic products. It is based in **Bern**. Legally it is a **federal public-law institution** and is assigned to the Federal Department of Home Affairs. This means it belongs to the Confederation but can work fairly independently.

Swissmedic started its work on 1 January 2002. At the same time, the **Therapeutic Products Act**, which governs the authority's work, came into force. Before that, the main responsibility lay with the **Intercantonal Office for the Control of Medicines**, which was run by the cantons. With Swissmedic, supervision was brought together at federal level for the whole of Switzerland.

A company that wants to sell a new medicine submits an **application for authorisation** to Swissmedic. Experts then check the documents for **quality, safety and effectiveness**. For example, they look at whether the medicine is made cleanly and whether the benefit is greater than the risks. Only after this check may the medicine be sold in Switzerland.

Even after authorisation, Swissmedic stays alert. Doctors, pharmacists and patients can report **side effects**, and Swissmedic evaluates these reports. If necessary, the authority can issue warnings or have a medicine taken off the market. It also inspects manufacturing companies and monitors **medical devices** such as plasters, syringes or pacemakers.

Swissmedic only decides whether a medicine may be sold. Whether the **basic insurance** of the health insurance fund pays for it is decided by the **Federal Office of Public Health**. For this, the medicine is added to the so-called list of pharmaceutical specialities. Swissmedic also works with authorities in other countries, for example to fight fakes.

Medicines from unknown online shops can be **fake** and contain dangerous substances. That is why Swissmedic warns against ordering medicines from unsafe websites. It is safe to buy medicines at a pharmacy or chemist's. If you have questions, the staff at the pharmacy will be happy to help.

begriffe.erklaerung: The general term for medicines and medical devices.
Official permission to sell a medicine.
An unwanted effect of a medicine.
An aid for health that does not work chemically, such as a plaster or a thermometer.

gewusst: Swissmedic also checks medicines for animals, for example for dogs, cats and cows.
A medicine needs its own authorisation in Switzerland, even if it is already allowed abroad.

teile.einleitung: The nitrogen cycle describes the path of the element nitrogen through the air, soil, water and living things. Nitrogen is found in every protein and in genetic material, but most living things cannot use the nitrogen from the air directly. Only certain bacteria, and humans with their technology, can convert it.
wichtigste: Dry air consists of about 78 per cent nitrogen.
Rhizobia fix nitrogen from the air in the root nodules of legumes.
The enzyme nitrogenase splits the stable triple bond of the nitrogen molecule.
The reddish leghaemoglobin keeps the oxygen level low in the nodules and so protects the nitrogenase.
Cyanobacteria fix a lot of nitrogen from the air in waters and rice fields.
Lightning during thunderstorms turns nitrogen from the air into a reactive form without any living things.
Since the beginning of the 20th century, the Haber-Bosch process has produced ammonia from nitrogen in the air.
In Switzerland, most ammonia emissions come from farming.

abschnitte.text: Dry air consists of about **78 per cent** nitrogen, chemically N₂. In it, two nitrogen atoms are joined by a very strong **triple bond**. That is why this nitrogen is very unreactive, and plants and animals cannot use it directly. Yet all living things need nitrogen to build proteins and genetic material.

Some microbes can turn nitrogen from the air into ammonium; this is called **nitrogen fixation**. In this process, the enzyme **nitrogenase** splits the triple bond. In the root nodules of legumes such as clover, peas, beans and soya live **rhizobia**, which do this for the plant. The reddish leghaemoglobin keeps the oxygen low there, because oxygen would destroy the nitrogenase.

**Lightning** during thunderstorms also turns some nitrogen from the air into a reactive form, which reaches the soil with the rain. In waters and rice fields, **cyanobacteria** fix a large part of the nitrogen from the air. Plants then take up the nitrogen through their roots, mainly as nitrate or ammonium. Animals and humans get it by eating plants or other animals.

When living things die or excrete faeces and urine, bacteria break the remains down into ammonium again. Other bacteria turn ammonium into nitrate; this is called **nitrification**. In **denitrification**, yet other bacteria turn nitrate back into nitrogen gas. So the nitrogen is back in the air, and the cycle starts all over again.

At the beginning of the 20th century, the German chemists Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed the **Haber-Bosch process**. In it, **ammonia** is produced from nitrogen in the air and hydrogen under high pressure and heat. It is used to make artificial fertiliser, which has greatly increased harvests around the world. Experts estimate that without this fertiliser about half of today's humanity could not be fed.

abschnitte.titel: Too much of a good thing
abschnitte.text: When too much nitrogen gets into the environment, problems arise. Nitrate can get into the groundwater, and in lakes nutrients encourage too much algae growth. In Switzerland, most **ammonia emissions** come from farming, especially from the slurry and manure of farm animals. Ammonia harms forests, moors and species-rich meadows because it over-fertilises them.

begriffe.erklaerung: Turning nitrogen from the air into a form that living things can use.
An enzyme in some bacteria that can split nitrogen from the air.
Bacteria that live in the root nodules of legumes and fix nitrogen.
A sharp-smelling gas made of nitrogen and hydrogen.
A nitrogen compound that plants can easily take up as a nutrient.

gewusst: Farmers sow clover or beans to fertilise the soil with nitrogen in a natural way.
Fritz Haber received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1918, and Carl Bosch in 1931.
If you cut open a root nodule of a pea, it is often pink inside.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Polar Institute is a Swiss organisation that supports research in the coldest regions on Earth. It was founded in 2016 and funds projects in the Arctic, in Antarctica and in high mountains. Although Switzerland has no sea, it is very strong in ice and glacier research.
wichtigste: The Swiss Polar Institute was founded in 2016.
It funds Swiss research in the Arctic, Antarctica and high mountain regions.
Its founders include EPFL and ETH Zurich.
The businessman Frederik Paulsen played a major part in supporting its foundation.
Its first big expedition was the Antarctic Circumnavigation Expedition.
Switzerland has observer status in the Arctic Council.
Switzerland has joined the Antarctic Treaty.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss Polar Institute, SPI for short, was founded in **2016**. Its founding institutions include **EPFL** in Lausanne and **ETH Zurich**, as well as other research institutes. The Swedish businessman and polar traveller **Frederik Paulsen**, who lives in Switzerland, played a major part in supporting its foundation. The institute is based in Sion in Valais.

One of the SPI's main tasks is to fund Swiss **research projects** in polar and high mountain regions. It gives money to researchers and helps plan difficult journeys into the ice. It also brings together experts from different universities. Training young polar researchers is important to it as well.

Its first big undertaking was the **Antarctic Circumnavigation Expedition**, ACE for short. From December 2016 to March 2017, a Russian research ship sailed all the way round Antarctica. On board were researchers from many countries with more than 20 projects. They studied the sea, islands, animals, air and ice around the **southern continent**.

The SPI expressly also studies **high mountain regions** such as the Alps or the Himalayas. Glaciers and permafrost in the mountains react to climate change just as sensitively as the ice of the polar regions. That is why people sometimes speak of the **Third Pole**. With its glaciers, Switzerland has a lot of experience in this field.

As early as 1912, the Swiss researcher **Alfred de Quervain** and his team crossed the Greenland ice sheet. Switzerland has joined the **Antarctic Treaty**, which reserves Antarctica for peace and science. In the **Arctic Council**, where the countries around the North Pole work together, Switzerland has observer status. This allows it to contribute its knowledge without being an Arctic state itself.

begriffe.erklaerung: The region around the North Pole with a lot of sea ice and the Arctic Ocean.
The region around the South Pole with the ice-covered continent of Antarctica.
A planned research journey to an area that is hard to reach.
Ground that stays frozen all year round, including in high mountains.

gewusst: Switzerland has no sea, but it is one of the leading countries in glacier and ice research.
On the ACE expedition, the research ship sailed once all the way round Antarctica.
Because of its huge amounts of ice, the high mountain region is sometimes called the Third Pole.

teile.einleitung: In ecology, succession is the natural sequence in which plants and animals settle in a habitat one after another. In this way, bare rock or an abandoned meadow can turn into a forest over many years.
wichtigste: Succession is the sequence over time of communities of living things in one place.
In primary succession, ground that previously had no life is colonised.
In secondary succession, a community forms anew, for example when a pasture becomes overgrown with bushes.
Lichens are among the first pioneers on bare rock.
On the Swiss Central Plateau, a beech forest would usually develop without humans.
Primary succession can be observed well in front of retreating glaciers.
The volcanic islands of Krakatoa and Surtsey are famous examples of resettlement.

abschnitte.text: The word **succession** comes from the Latin succedere, to follow. It means that plants and animals replace one another in a place. First come undemanding **pioneer species**, and later bigger and more demanding species follow. At the end there is often a stable **climax community**, which does not change much for a long time. On the Swiss Central Plateau, without human interference, this would usually be a beech forest.

In **primary succession**, life begins on ground where nothing grew before, such as bare rock or fresh lava. **Lichens** and mosses are the first to settle. They slowly break down the rock, and with dead plant remains a thin layer of soil forms. Later grasses, herbs, shrubs and finally trees can grow on it.

Because the glaciers in the Alps are retreating, new bare areas appear every year. In the **glacier foreland** you can observe primary succession as if along a timeline. Close to the ice only a few pioneer plants grow, further away small willows and larches, and further still a proper forest. At the Morteratsch Glacier in the Engadine, signs along the footpath show where the ice was in which year.

In **secondary succession**, the soil is already there, but the old plant cover has been destroyed or is no longer used. An example is an abandoned pasture that gradually becomes overgrown with bushes and turns into forest. After the storm **Lothar** in December 1999, large areas of forest in Switzerland were flattened. On some of these areas, researchers have since been observing how the forest grows back by itself. **Silting up**, in which a lake gradually fills with plants and mud, is also a form of succession.

In 1883 a huge volcanic eruption destroyed a large part of the island of **Krakatoa** in Indonesia, and all life there was wiped out. Researchers then observed how plants and animals settled on the island again. In 1963 the volcanic island of **Surtsey** rose out of the sea off Iceland. Only a few researchers are allowed to set foot on it, so that the natural colonisation can be followed undisturbed. Seeds and animals reached the island with the wind, with the sea and with birds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that is one of the first to settle in a new habitat.
A stable community of living things at the end of a succession, often a forest.
A partnership of a fungus and an alga that can grow even on bare rock.
The gradual filling of a lake with plants and sediment.

gewusst: Surtsey has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008, because the development of life on new land can be observed there.
Without mowing and grazing, most meadows in Switzerland would turn into forest within a few decades.

teile.einleitung: The sample size states how many people or things are included in a study. After all, you cannot always ask every person or test every screw in a factory. How large a sample has to be for the result to be reliable is one of the most important questions in statistics.
wichtigste: The sample size is abbreviated with the letter n.
With sample size planning, you calculate before a study starts how many participants are needed to prove an effect.
The smaller the effect you want to prove, the larger the sample has to be.
In clinical trials, researchers often aim for a statistical power of 80 per cent.
According to the law of large numbers, the mean approaches the expected value as the sample grows.
For a margin of error of 2 percentage points you need about 2400 respondents.
A biased selection is not repaired by a large sample.

abschnitte.text: A **sample** is a selection from a larger group, the population. The **sample size** n says how many elements this selection includes. From the sample you want to draw conclusions about the whole group, for example in surveys, medicine trials or quality checks. As a rule, the larger n is, the more accurate the result.

If you toss a coin only ten times, it can easily land on heads seven times. If you toss it a thousand times, the proportion is almost always close to half. This is described by the **law of large numbers**: as the sample grows, the mean approaches the expected value. Small samples, on the other hand, are prone to random outliers.

Surveys often state a **margin of error**. For a margin of error of 2 percentage points, with 95 per cent certainty and a proportion of around 50 per cent, you need about 2400 respondents. For 3 percentage points, roughly 1000 respondents are enough. If you want to halve the margin of error, you have to make the sample about four times as large.

Before a medical study, **sample size planning** is used to calculate how many participants are needed. The smaller the expected effect, the more participants are needed. Researchers often aim for a **statistical power** of 80 per cent, meaning a good chance of actually finding a real effect. Because some participants drop out, more are planned for: if you need 200 and expect 20 per cent to drop out, you include at least 250.

In 1936 the US magazine **Literary Digest** surveyed millions of people and received over two million replies. It still predicted the wrong winner of the election, because the people asked were mainly better-off. The pollster George Gallup got it right with a much smaller but well-chosen sample. The lesson: a biased selection is not repaired by size.

Small studies that achieve a significant result often **overestimate** the size of the effect. With few participants, only effects that happen to be large reach the threshold of significance. Later, larger studies therefore often find smaller effects. That is why experts prefer to rely on several large studies rather than on a single small one.

begriffe.erklaerung: A selection from a larger group that is studied.
The whole group that you want to know something about.
The range in which the true value probably lies.
The probability of actually detecting an effect that really exists in a study.
A result that very probably did not come about just by chance.

gewusst: Whether you want to describe 10,000 or 10 million people makes hardly any difference to the sample size needed.
In the census, people used to try to count really everyone, a so-called full survey.
In Switzerland, the Federal Statistical Office today adds sample surveys to its register data.

teile.einleitung: A tally chart is a simple way of keeping track while counting, by making a mark for each thing you count. Because you always group five marks into a bundle, you can quickly read off the result at the end.
wichtigste: With a tally chart you can count along quickly.
You make four upright marks and draw the fifth one across them.
This creates bundles of five, which you can count more quickly.
For the number 10 you need two bundles of five.
The number 7 is one bundle of five and two single marks.
Two bundles of five and three marks make 13.
Tally marks are among the oldest ways of recording numbers.

abschnitte.text: A **tally chart** helps you count things that come past one after another. For each thing you make an upright mark. After four marks you draw the fifth one **across** them, which creates a **bundle of five**. Then you start a new bundle next to it.

Instead of counting each mark separately, you count the bundles in steps of five: 5, 10, 15 and so on. Then you add the remaining single marks. So three bundles of five and one mark make 16. If Lea has four bundles of five while counting red cars, she has seen 20 red cars. Five is handy because we have five fingers on one hand.

Tally charts are used in traffic counts, for counting birds or for a vote in class. If Tim counts 8 blackbirds and 12 sparrows in the garden, he can see straight away in his chart that there are 4 more sparrows. When playing the card game Jass, points are often written down with marks too. A tally chart can then easily be turned into a **table** or a bar chart.

Tens of thousands of years ago, people were already carving notches into bones, probably to count something. A famous example is the **Ishango bone** from Central Africa with many carved notches. In the Middle Ages, people in Switzerland also used the **tally stick**, on which debts were recorded with notches. This is where the German saying “etwas auf dem Kerbholz haben” (to have something on the tally stick, meaning to have done something wrong) comes from.

Tally charts do not look the same everywhere. In China, Japan and Korea, people often write the character 正 when counting, which is made of exactly five strokes. In other countries, some people draw a square with a diagonal, which also makes five strokes. But the idea is the same everywhere: you combine marks into **groups**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A counting aid in which you make a mark for each thing you count.
Four upright marks with one mark across them, five altogether.
A wooden stick into which people used to carve notches to count debts.
A picture in which amounts are shown as bars of different heights.

gewusst: The Roman numerals I, II, III and V probably go back to old tally marks and notches.
Prisoners in films often count their days with tally marks on the wall.

teile.einleitung: A synapse is the point of contact between two nerve cells or between a nerve cell and a muscle cell. Here a signal is passed on from one cell to the next, usually with the help of chemical messengers. Without synapses we could neither think nor move nor learn anything.
wichtigste: A synapse connects two nerve cells or a nerve cell with a muscle cell.
Between the two cells there is a tiny gap, the synaptic cleft.
The messengers are called neurotransmitters and are stored in small vesicles at the end of the axon.
Acetylcholine transmits signals from the nerves to the skeletal muscles.
Dopamine is closely linked to the brain's reward system, while GABA mainly has an inhibiting effect.
The term “synapse” was coined by Charles Sherrington at the end of the 19th century.
There are about 100 trillion synapses in the human brain.

abschnitte.text: Nerve cells, also called **neurons**, pass on information as electrical signals. Every nerve cell has a long extension, the **axon**, through which it sends out signals. At the end of the axon is the synapse, where the signal is handed over to the next cell. A single nerve cell can be connected to other cells by thousands of synapses.

When an electrical signal arrives at the end of the axon, small **vesicles** merge with the cell wall. They release their messengers into the **synaptic cleft**. This gap is only about 20 to 40 millionths of a millimetre wide. On the other side, the messengers dock onto matching docking sites, the **receptors**, and trigger a new signal there. Afterwards the messengers are quickly broken down or taken back up.

There are dozens of different **neurotransmitters** with different tasks. **Acetylcholine** makes our muscles contract when the brain gives the command. **Dopamine** plays a role in joy, motivation and reward. GABA slows the nerve cells down and so makes sure that the brain is not overstimulated. Serotonin affects mood and sleep, among other things.

Synapses are not fixed but can become stronger or weaker. This ability is called **synaptic plasticity**. When you practise something often, the connections involved in the brain become stronger. Synapses that are rarely used, on the other hand, can be broken down again. This is how our memory is formed, and how we learn, for example, to ride a bike or learn vocabulary.

The British researcher **Charles Sherrington** gave the point of contact the name synapse in 1897, after a Greek word for “to join”. Before that, the Spaniard Santiago Ramón y Cajal had shown with the microscope that nerve cells are individual cells. Only with the **electron microscope** in the 1950s could the synaptic cleft really be seen. Several Nobel Prizes have been awarded for discoveries about the synapse.

Many medicines work directly at the synapses, for example medicines against pain, anxiety or depression. Some **poisons** also act here, for example the arrow poison curare, which blocks the transmission to the muscles. In Parkinson's disease, dopamine is lacking in the brain. That is why research into synapses is very important for medicine.

begriffe.erklaerung: A nerve cell that receives and passes on signals.
The long extension of a nerve cell through which it sends out signals.
A chemical messenger that transmits a signal at the synapse.
The tiny gap between two cells at a synapse.
A docking site to which only a matching messenger can bind, like a key in a lock.

gewusst: With about 100 trillion synapses, the brain has far more connections than there are stars in our Milky Way.
At a chemical synapse, a signal needs only about a thousandth of a second to cross the gap.
As well as chemical synapses, there are also electrical synapses, in which the current flows directly from cell to cell.

teile.einleitung: In German the word “teilen” has two meanings: in maths it means splitting an amount into equal parts, which is also called dividing. In everyday life it means sharing, giving others some of what you have. Both have to do with fairness and living together.
wichtigste: When you share fairly, everyone gets the same amount.
If you share 6 jelly babies fairly with a friend, each of you gets 3.
If you divide 12 cherries among 4 children, each one gets 3.
A toy that everyone wants can be shared by taking turns.
In a library, many people share the same books.
When several people share a car, it is called car sharing.
Some animals, such as vampire bats, also share their food.

abschnitte.text: In maths, dividing is also called **division**. The calculation 12 : 4 = 3 means: 12 cherries shared fairly among 4 children gives 3 cherries per child. The number being divided is called the **dividend**, the number you divide by is called the divisor, and the result is called the **quotient**. Dividing is the opposite of multiplying, because 3 times 4 makes 12 again.

abschnitte.titel: When it does not work out exactly
abschnitte.text: Not every division works out exactly. If you share 7 jelly babies between 2 children, each gets 3, and 1 jelly baby is left over; this is the **remainder**. You can also cut the last one in half, and then each gets three and a half. By the way, you cannot divide by zero at all; it is not allowed in maths.

In everyday life, sharing means giving others something or using something together. If everyone wants the same toy, you can **take turns**. It is fair when everyone gets the same amount or everyone gets a turn for the same length of time. The German saying “Geteilte Freude ist doppelte Freude” (shared joy is double joy) says that experiencing things together makes people happy.

In a **library**, many people borrow the same books one after another. In Switzerland there are also **toy libraries**, where you can borrow games and toys. In **car sharing**, several people share a car; in Switzerland the cooperative Mobility is well known for this. Using things together saves money, space and raw materials.

Animals sometimes share too. **Vampire bats** in Central and South America give some of their food to hungry members of their group. They mainly help those who have helped them in the past. Chimpanzees also share food, and ants feed one another. Researchers see in this the roots of cooperation and fairness.

begriffe.erklaerung: Calculating by dividing, for example 12 : 4 = 3.
The result of a division.
What is left over when a division does not work out exactly.
Several people use the same car together.
A place where you can borrow games and toys; in Switzerland it is called a “Ludothek”.

gewusst: A vampire bat can survive only a few nights without food, so sharing is vital for it.
The sign “:” for dividing is usual in Switzerland; in other countries people often write “÷” or a fraction line.
Even small children notice very clearly when something is shared out unfairly.

teile.einleitung: Synthetic biology is a young field of research between biology, chemistry and engineering. Researchers try to design and rebuild living things such as bacteria or yeasts in a targeted way so that they gain new properties. In doing so they often work like engineers who put a machine together from components.
wichtigste: The aim of synthetic biology is to design and build biological systems with new properties in a targeted way.
In 2010 Craig Venter's team was the first to run a bacterium with genetic material made entirely in the laboratory.
The minimal cell JCVI-syn3.0, presented in 2016, managed with only 473 genes.
Modified baker's yeast is used to produce a precursor of the malaria drug artemisinin.
The repressilator of 2000 was an artificial gene circuit that produces oscillations in bacteria.
Students from all over the world compete in the iGEM competition, including teams from ETH Zurich.
A kill switch is meant to make sure that artificially modified organisms die outside the laboratory.

abschnitte.text: In synthetic biology, genes are seen as **building blocks** that can be combined. A gene is a section of DNA that contains a set of instructions, usually for a protein. Researchers write new DNA sections on the computer and have them made in the laboratory. They then put these into cells so that the cells carry out new tasks. Unlike classic genetic engineering, whole **gene circuits** or even whole genomes are often newly designed.

In 2000 Michael Elowitz and Stanislas Leibler presented the **repressilator**. In it, three genes inhibit each other in a circle, so that the bacteria regularly blink on and off. At the same time, a genetic toggle switch was built that can switch between two states. Such circuits work in a similar way to electronic circuits in a computer.

In 2010 **Craig Venter's** team put genetic material assembled in the laboratory into a bacterium, and the cell lived and divided. In 2016 came the **minimal cell** JCVI-syn3.0 with only 473 genes, fewer than any other known free-living organism. In the international project Sc2.0, the entire genetic material of baker's yeast is being rebuilt. In 2019 researchers presented hachimoji DNA, which contains eight different bases instead of four.

A well-known example is the malaria drug **artemisinin**, which is originally obtained from sweet wormwood. Modified baker's yeast can produce a precursor of it, which makes the supply less dependent on harvests. Other aims are bacteria that detect diseases, break down pollutants or produce fuels and plastics. Insulin, too, has long been produced by modified microorganisms.

In the **iGEM** competition, students build their own biological systems from standardised building blocks. Teams from all over the world, including from ETH Zurich, present their projects every year. In Switzerland, for example, the ETH Department of Biosystems in Basel does research in synthetic biology. In this way young researchers learn how to plan biology like an engineering project.

Because new living things are created, **biosafety** is very important. A built-in **kill switch** is meant to make organisms die if they escape from the laboratory. Many people discuss how far we may change life and who sets the rules. In Switzerland, strict laws apply to work with modified organisms.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of DNA that contains instructions for the cell.
The entire genetic material of a living thing.
Several genes that control each other like the parts of an electronic circuit.
A cell with as few genes as possible that can just about stay alive.
A built-in self-destruct switch that makes modified organisms die outside the laboratory.

gewusst: Watermarks with names and quotations in DNA code were even built into the artificial genetic material of Venter's bacterium so that it could be identified.
The minimal cell JCVI-syn3.0 has fewer genes than many natural bacteria that live as parasites.
Several hundred teams from dozens of countries take part in iGEM every year.

teile.einleitung: The South Pole is the southernmost point on Earth. It lies in the middle of Antarctica on a huge sheet of ice, and from there every direction leads north. It is one of the coldest and loneliest places in the world.
wichtigste: The South Pole lies on the ice of Antarctica, about 2800 metres above sea level.
From the South Pole, you go north in every direction.
It is colder at the South Pole than at the North Pole, about minus 50 degrees on average over the year.
Roald Amundsen was the first to reach the South Pole, in 1911.
The Briton Robert Scott reached it in 1912 and died on the way back.
The marker is put in a new place every year, because the ice beneath it moves.
For photos there is a shiny ball surrounded by flags.

abschnitte.text: The geographic South Pole is the point where the imaginary **Earth's axis** passes through the surface in the south. It lies on a wide, flat plateau of **Antarctica**, far from the coast. Below the surface there is a layer of ice about 2700 metres thick, which is why the pole is about 2800 metres high. All lines of longitude meet here, and every step leads north.

It is much colder at the South Pole than at the North Pole, because it lies high up and is not surrounded by sea. On average over the year the temperature is about minus 50 degrees, and in winter often below minus 60 degrees. Very little snow falls, which is why Antarctica is regarded as a **cold desert**. For half the year the sun does not set, and for the other half it is dark.

In 1911 two expeditions tried to be the first to reach the South Pole. The Norwegian **Roald Amundsen** arrived with dog sledges on 14 December 1911. The Briton **Robert Scott** reached the pole about five weeks later, on 17 January 1912, and found Amundsen's tent there. Scott and his companions died on the way back from cold, hunger and exhaustion.

Since 1956 the USA has run the **Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station** right at the pole. In summer more than a hundred people work there, in winter only a small group that cannot leave for months. They study the weather, the ice, space and tiny particles from space. The station is supplied by aircraft that land on skis.

Next to the station is the **ceremonial South Pole**, a shiny ball on a stand surrounded by flags, where visitors take photos. The exact geographic pole is marked with a metal post. Because the ice moves about ten metres every year, this post is put in a new place at the beginning of each year. Every year the researchers design a new plaque for it.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ice-covered continent around the South Pole.
An imaginary line around which the Earth turns.
An imaginary line from pole to pole that is used to give the position of places on Earth.
An area where it is very cold and hardly any precipitation falls.

gewusst: The South Pole has no time zone of its own; the station uses New Zealand time.
The magnetic South Pole, which a compass reacts to, is not at the geographic South Pole.
Xavier Mertz from Basel took part in an Australian Antarctic expedition from 1911 to 1913 and lost his life on it.
